articles.title: Whose praise do I want?

statement.t: Before I want anyone’s praise I look into their mind; praise makes me no better, and fame after death is nothing to me.

parts.words: Before I want anyone’s praise I look into their mind
fame after death is nothing to me

statement.kind: One question answered from three sides
statement.form: The section asks whose praise is worth wanting. Claims 1 and 2 answer from the people who give it: look into them, and I find that they judge even themselves badly. Claim 5 answers from the thing praised: praise does not change it. Claim 3 answers from time: those who would remember me die too. Claim 4 shows what wanting praise does to me. The statement takes one part from the first three answers.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, three claims gain a second author: seeing what sort of people they are (claim 1), not wanting praise from people I cannot praise (claim 2), and taking others’ word for what I am (claim 4). The article gains an audience of a few, one or none; a way to assess judgments; and a way back: what I seem to myself counts for more. He challenges two claims: he holds that those who come after will judge without ill will, and that deserved praise from good people is a good.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement gains a clause: what I seem to myself matters far more than what I seem to others. Its last part stands only in the sense that the talk of those who come after will not concern me; Seneca’s school holds that renown after death is a good, and so would deny that fame after death is worth nothing.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: when you want to make a true valuation of a human being and to know what he is like, examine him naked
piece.follows: To know what a person is worth and what kind of person they are, I should look at them stripped of all their trappings.
piece.context: Letter 76: we value a man along with the things he is decked out with. To know his worth, Seneca says, strip away his estate, his offices, even his body, and look at his mind.
gives: see what sort of people they are

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Why are you glad to have been praised by these people, whom you cannot yourself praise?
piece.follows: It makes no sense to be glad of praise from people I could not praise myself.
piece.context: Letter 52, on choosing teachers: a lecturer leaves cheerful at the shouts of the ignorant. By “these people” Seneca means that audience, whom he could not praise himself.
gives: I do not want praise from such people

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: as it is, you take the word of others for what you are
piece.follows: Lucilius takes other people’s word for what he is, instead of looking at himself within.
piece.context: Letter 80: a king’s worth shows once the band on his head is undone. Seneca tells Lucilius to weigh himself up by looking at himself within, not by what others report.
gives: I value their judgment of me above my own

items.label: action
items.role: An audience of few or none
items.t: I despise the pleasure that the approval of the many gives. It is enough for me if what I do reaches a few people, or one, or none.
items.why: Marcus asks whose praise is worth wanting and answers by looking at those who give it. He does not say how many people I need. Seneca says: a few, one or none.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: so that you may despise the pleasure that comes from the approval of the greater number
support.follows: These sayings are meant to make me despise the pleasure that the approval of the greater number gives.
support.context: The close of Letter 7, on crowds, after three sayings about needing few listeners or none. Seneca tells Lucilius what the sayings are for.
gives: I despise the pleasure that the approval of the many gives

support.author: seneca
support.quote: A few are enough for me, one is enough, none is enough.
support.follows: A few people, one person or no one at all is enough for the one who said this.
support.context: Letter 7, on crowds: a man was asked why he worked so hard at an art that would reach very few people. This was his answer.
gives: It is enough for me if what I do reaches a few people, or one, or none

items.label: practice
items.t: I assess people’s judgments and do not count them. How a person praises and is praised shows me what kind of person they are.
items.why: Claim 1 looks into the ruling parts of those whose praise I might want. Seneca says what to look for there: how they praise and are praised, and the worth of a judgment rather than the number of voices.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: that you assess judgments and do not count them
support.follows: Philosophy teaches me to assess what people judge, not to count how many judge so.
support.context: Letter 29: what philosophy will do for Lucilius. The “judgments” are what people think of him; Seneca would pity him if the whole city cheered him.
gives: I assess people’s judgments and do not count them

support.author: seneca
support.quote: you will know what each person is like if you look at how he praises and how he is praised.
support.follows: How someone praises and how they are praised shows what kind of person they are.
support.context: Letter 52: the shouting of the theatre should differ from that of the school. Small signs show character, Seneca says, and praise shows it best.
gives: How a person praises and is praised shows me what kind of person they are

items.label: breaks
items.role: The price, and the way back
items.t: To win the people’s favour I would have to use bad arts and make myself like them. What I seem to myself matters far more than what I seem to others.
items.why: Claim 4 shows how wanting others’ good opinion sets me against myself, and gives no way back. Seneca names the price, becoming like the people, and the way back: my own view of myself counts for more.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The favour of the people is sought by bad arts. You must make yourself like those people
support.follows: Winning the people’s favour takes bad arts, and it means making oneself like those people.
support.context: Letter 29: Seneca has just cited a saying of Epicurus about not wishing to please the people. By “those people” he means the people whose favour is sought, who approve only of those they recognise.
gives: To win the people’s favour I would have to use bad arts and make myself like them

support.author: seneca
support.quote: But what you seem to yourself matters far more than what you seem to others
support.follows: What I seem to myself matters far more than what I seem to others.
support.context: Letter 29, on not pleasing the people: having said that their favour is won only by becoming like them, Seneca sets what one seems to oneself above what one seems to others.
gives: What I seem to myself matters far more than what I seem to others

items.t: Seneca disagrees about those who come after. Marcus says they will be people like those I find hard to bear now; Seneca says they will judge me without ill will and without favour, and that I should look to them; his school holds that renown after death is a good. He agrees with Marcus that the talk of those who come after will not concern us. He is not consistent: in Ep. 113.32 he says it is nothing to the point how many people know that I am just.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The man who thinks of the people of his own time is born for few. Many thousands of years, many thousands of peoples will come after: look to those.
support.follows: Whoever thinks of the people of their own time lives for few; I should look to the many peoples that will come after me.
support.context: Letter 79: fame is the shadow of virtue and may come late, once envy is gone. By “those” Seneca means the many peoples who will come after Lucilius.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: there will come those who judge without ill will, without favour
support.follows: Later generations will judge me without ill will and without favour.
support.context: Letter 79, on fame that comes late: envy may silence everyone of one’s own day. By “those who judge” Seneca means people of later generations.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The talk of those who come after will indeed not concern us at all
support.follows: What those who come after say of us will not concern us.
support.context: Letter 79, on fame that comes late. Seneca grants that the dead will not feel what those who come after say of them, and holds that it will still honour them.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: the renown which comes after death is a good
support.follows: Seneca’s school holds that renown after death is a good.
support.context: Letter 102 takes up an argument from an earlier letter, in which Seneca set out to prove what his school holds, that renown after death is a good.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: it is nothing to the point how many people know of your fairness
support.follows: How many people know that I am fair is nothing to the point.
support.context: The close of Letter 113, on justice that seeks no reward. By “your fairness” Seneca means being just; how many people know of it, he says, does not matter.

items.t: Seneca disagrees that my good is only my own action and never another person’s activity. Praise given to a good man by good men, when he deserves it, is a good, and it is his own good as well as theirs (Ep. 102.18–19). He agrees that the many are not the judges: glory rests on their judgments, renown on the judgments of the good (Ep. 102.17).

support.author: seneca
support.quote: It is mine, as the one who is praised: because nature bore me as someone who loves all people, I both rejoice to have done good and am glad to have found grateful interpreters of the virtues.
support.follows: Being praised by good people is my own good as the one praised: since nature made me someone who loves all people, I rejoice to have done good and am glad to have found people who are grateful for it.
support.context: Letter 102: renown is praise given to a good man by good men. Asked whose good it is, the one praised or the ones praising, Seneca answers: both.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: So to be praised deservedly is a good of both
support.follows: Praise given to someone who deserves it is a good both for the one praised and for those who praise.
support.context: Letter 102: to praise the deserving is an act of justice, so it is a good of the one who praises and of the one praised. By “both” Seneca means the one praised and those who praise.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: glory is made up of the judgments of the many, renown of the judgments of the good.
support.follows: Glory is made up of what the many judge; renown of what the good judge.
support.context: Letter 102 separates renown from glory. Glory is made up of the judgments of the many; by “the good” Seneca means good men, whose judgments make up renown.

passages.title: On learning in old age, and virtue as the only good
passages.text: This is the error we suffer from, this is how we are taken in: we value no one by what he is, but add to him the things he is decked out with as well. Yet when you want to make a true valuation of a human being and to know what he is like, examine him naked; let him lay aside his estate, let him lay aside his offices and the other lies of fortune, let him strip off even his body: look at his mind, what it is like and how great, whether it is great by what is another’s or by what is its own.

passages.title: On choosing guides and applauding philosophers
passages.text: And how great is the madness of the man whom the shouts of the ignorant send away from the lecture hall cheerful! Why are you glad to have been praised by these people, whom you cannot yourself praise? Fabianus used to lecture to the public, but he was listened to with restraint; from time to time a great shout of praise would break out, but one that the greatness of what he was saying had called forth, not the sound of speech that had glided by softly and without a stumble.

passages.title: On training the mind and false happiness
passages.text: Do you see that king of Scythia or Sarmatia, adorned with the mark of rank on his head? If you want to value him and to know what he is like through and through, undo the band: much that is bad lies hidden under it. Why do I speak of others? If you want to weigh yourself up, set aside money, house, standing; look at yourself within, for yourself: as it is, you take the word of others for what you are. Farewell.

passages.title: On avoiding the crowd
passages.text: These things, my Lucilius, are to be stored away in your mind, so that you may despise the pleasure that comes from the approval of the greater number. Many praise you: have you any reason to be pleased with yourself, if you are the kind of man whom many understand? Let your good things face inward. Farewell.

passages.title: On avoiding the crowd
passages.text: That man too put it well, whoever he was (for it is disputed who said it): when he was asked what was the aim of such great care over an art that would reach very few, he said, “A few are enough for me, one is enough, none is enough.” Epicurus put this third one excellently, when he was writing to one of the partners in his studies: “I write these things,” he said, “not for many, but for you; for we are a large enough theatre, each for the other.”

passages.title: On giving advice only to the willing
passages.text: What, then, will that philosophy deliver, which is praised and is to be preferred to all arts and all things? This, of course: that you would rather please yourself than the people, that you assess judgments and do not count them, that you live without fear of gods and men, that you either overcome evils or end them. But if I see you celebrated by the approving voices of the crowd, if when you come in there is a din of shouting and applause, the honours of a pantomime dancer, if throughout the whole city women and children praise you, why should I not pity you, since I know what road leads to that favour? Farewell.

passages.title: On choosing guides and applauding philosophers
passages.text: Let there be some difference between the shouting of the theatre and that of the school: there is a certain good taste in praising too. Everything is a sign of everything, if it is watched, and one may take evidence of character even from the smallest things: the lewd man is shown by his walk, by a movement of his hand, sometimes by a single answer, by a finger brought to his head, by the turn of his eyes; the wicked man is given away by his laugh, the madman by his face and bearing. For those traits come out into the open through their marks: you will know what each person is like if you look at how he praises and how he is praised.

passages.title: On giving advice only to the willing
passages.text: “Who said this?” you ask, as if you did not know whom I order to pay. Epicurus. But all of them, from every house, will shout this same thing to you together: Peripatetics, Academics, Stoics, Cynics. For who can please the people if virtue pleases him? The favour of the people is sought by bad arts. You must make yourself like those people: they will not approve of you unless they recognise you. But what you seem to yourself matters far more than what you seem to others; the love of base people cannot be won except by base means.

passages.title: On Etna, virtue and late fame
passages.text: No virtue lies hidden, and to have lain hidden is not virtue’s own loss: a day will come to make public the virtue that was buried and held down by the spite of its own age. The man who thinks of the people of his own time is born for few. Many thousands of years, many thousands of peoples will come after: look to those. Even if envy has imposed silence on all who are alive with you, there will come those who judge without ill will, without favour. If virtue has any reward from fame, this does not perish either. The talk of those who come after will indeed not concern us at all; yet it will honour us and keep returning to us even though we do not feel it.

passages.title: On fame after death and the soul’s immortality
passages.text: You say that in my earlier letter I did not work through the whole inquiry in which I was trying to prove what our school holds: that the renown which comes after death is a good. For, you say, I did not resolve the objection that is made against us: “No good,” they say, “is made up of things that stand apart; but this one is made up of things that stand apart.”

passages.title: On whether the virtues are living beings
passages.text: Fix in yourself as well what I was saying a little earlier: that it is nothing to the point how many people know of your fairness. Anyone who wants his virtue made public is working not for virtue but for glory. Are you unwilling to be just without glory? But, by Hercules, you will often have to be just with a bad name, and then, if you are wise, let a bad reputation well won delight you. Farewell.

passages.title: On fame after death and the soul’s immortality
passages.text: “Whose good,” he says, “is renown, that is, praise rendered to a good man by good men? Is it the good of the one praised or of the one praising?” Of both. It is mine, as the one who is praised: because nature bore me as someone who loves all people, I both rejoice to have done good and am glad to have found grateful interpreters of the virtues. That they are grateful is a good of several people, but it is mine too. For my mind is so made that I judge the good of others to be mine, at any rate the good of those for whom I am myself the cause of the good.

passages.title: On fame after death and the soul’s immortality
passages.text: That is a good of those who praise, for it is done by virtue, and every act of virtue is a good. This could not have come to them unless I were such a man. So to be praised deservedly is a good of both, just as much, by Hercules, as to have judged well is a good of the one who judges and of the one in whose favour judgment was given. Surely you do not doubt that justice is both a good of the one who has it and also a good of the one to whom it pays what is owed? To praise one who deserves it is justice; therefore it is a good of both.

passages.title: On fame after death and the soul’s immortality
passages.text: Fame in any case needs a voice; renown can come even without a voice, content with a judgment. It is complete not only among people who are silent but even among people who cry out against it. I will say what the difference is between renown and glory: glory is made up of the judgments of the many, renown of the judgments of the good.

claims.t: Before I want to please people or fear them as judges, I look right into their ruling parts and see what sort of people they are: what they are after and what they run from, and what they are like when they eat and sleep.
claims.shared: Three passages give the same instruction: look into “their ruling parts” (9.32, 9.16, 4.31). 6.54 and 10.20 open with the same Greek words, “what sort of people those are” and “what they are like”, and 9.32 asks me to see their “little souls naked”. What they are after is in both 9.32 (“what sort of things they are in earnest about”) and 4.31 (“what sort of things they chase”).
claims.changed: The passages mostly speak of “these people” or “they”; the claim names them as those whose praise or judgment I care about, as 9.32, 9.16 and 6.54 do. “And at the wise as well” in 4.31 is left out, because its point is open: the wise may be a model to set against them, or more people to look into. The claim takes the “they” of 4.31, who run from and chase things, to be everyone looked at, not the wise alone; the translators allow both readings. Of 10.20’s list, eating and sleeping are kept. The statement says “mind” where the claim keeps the passages’ “ruling parts”.

support.quote: What the ruling parts of these people are, what sort of things they are in earnest about, and what sort of things win their love and honour.
support.follows: I should consider what rules in these people, what they take seriously, and what they give their love and honour for.
gives: I look right into their ruling parts
what they are after

support.quote: Think of yourself as looking at their little souls naked.
support.follows: I should picture their small souls stripped bare, as they really are.
gives: see what sort of people they are

support.quote: Pass inside, right inside, into their ruling parts, and you will see what judges you are afraid of
support.follows: If I go deep into these people’s ruling parts, I will see what kind of judges I am afraid of.
gives: fear them as judges
I look right into their ruling parts

support.quote: Look closely into their ruling parts, and at the wise as well: what sort of things they run from, and what sort of things they chase.
support.follows: I should look closely into people’s ruling parts, and at the wise too, and see what they run from and what they chase.
gives: I look right into their ruling parts
what they are after
what they run from

support.quote: What sort of people those are whom they want to please, and for what sort of gains, and through what sort of activities.
support.follows: Anyone who wants to please people should consider what those people are like, what is gained, and what has to be done for it.
gives: Before I want to please people
see what sort of people they are

support.quote: What they are like when eating, sleeping, mating, emptying their bowels, and the rest.
support.follows: I should picture these people as they are when they eat, sleep, mate and empty their bowels.
gives: see what sort of people they are
what they are like when they eat and sleep

claims.t: The people whose praise I might want judge even themselves badly: they curse themselves, they are not pleased with themselves, and they do not know where they are or who they are. I do not want praise from such people.
claims.shared: 9.16 and 8.51 both turn from what these people think of me to what they think of themselves: 9.16 shows “what sort of judges they are of themselves as well”, and 8.51 names a person who “curses themselves” and “is not pleased with themselves”.
claims.changed: 9.16 says “what sort of judges”; that they judge themselves badly is the sense its context gives, and 8.51 says it outright. 8.51 asks questions (“Do you want to be praised by…?”); the claim gives the answer they expect.

support.quote: and what sort of judges they are of themselves as well.
support.follows: Looking into these people also shows what kind of judges they are of themselves.
gives: judge even themselves badly

support.quote: Do you want to be praised by a person who curses themselves three times an hour? Do you want to please a person who is not pleased with themselves?
support.follows: It makes no sense to want praise from someone who curses themselves, or to want to please someone who is not pleased with themselves.
gives: judge even themselves badly
they curse themselves, they are not pleased with themselves
I do not want praise from such people

support.quote: people who know neither where they are nor who they are
support.follows: The people who clap know neither where they are nor who they are.
gives: they do not know where they are or who they are

claims.t: I do not chase fame after death; I make a gift of the present time to myself. Those who would remember me will be people like the ones I find hard to bear now, and they too are mortal: each of them will very soon die, and those after them too, until the whole memory goes out; and whatever they say or think of me is nothing to me.
claims.shared: 8.42 and 4.16 both say that those who chase “fame after death” fail to reckon that the people who would remember them are mortal: “those people too are mortal” (8.42), “each of those who remember them will very soon die too” (4.16).
claims.changed: Both passages describe other people who chase fame after death; the claim says that I do not. 4.16 goes on to suppose that the memory never dies; that case is kept apart, under “If I doubt it”.

support.quote: Look: make a gift of this present time to yourself.
support.follows: I should give the time that is here now to myself.
gives: I make a gift of the present time to myself

support.quote: People who instead chase fame after death do not take into account that those people will be others of the same kind as these whom they find hard to bear; and those people too are mortal.
support.follows: Those who would praise me later will be like the people I find hard to bear now, and they will die too.
gives: I do not chase fame after death
Those who would remember me will be people like the ones I find hard to bear now
they too are mortal

support.quote: Whoever is worked up about fame after death does not picture that each of those who remember them will very soon die too; then in turn the one who takes over from that one, until the whole memory also goes out
support.follows: Everyone who remembers me will soon die, and the one after them too, until all memory of me is gone.
gives: I do not chase fame after death
they too are mortal
each of them will very soon die
until the whole memory goes out

support.quote: And what is it to you at all, if those people echo with sounds of such a kind, or hold a judgment of such a kind about you?
support.follows: What later people say about me, or what they think of me, is nothing to me.
gives: whatever they say or think of me is nothing to me

claims.t: When I want other people’s good opinion, I go against myself. I love myself more than anyone, yet I value their judgment of me above my own; I look down on people, yet I fawn on them; I will not speak well of those who live beside me, yet I want those who come after to speak well of me.
claims.shared: Each passage sets what people give others against what they want from them, and the two do not agree: 12.3 and 6.17 join the two halves with “yet”, and 11.13 with “Despising one another, they fawn on one another”. “I go against myself” is the editor’s name for the contradiction that each of the three shows in its own words.
claims.changed: The passages speak of “each person” (12.3) and of “they” (11.13, 6.17); the claim says “I”. 11.13’s second pair (wanting to be above others, taking the lower place), 12.3’s test of the god or teacher and its sentence on shame, and the last sentence of 6.17 are left out.

support.quote: each person loves themselves more than everyone else, yet sets less value on their own judgment about themselves than on that of others
support.follows: People love themselves more than anyone, yet they value others’ judgment of them more than their own.
gives: I go against myself
I love myself more than anyone, yet I value their judgment of me above my own

support.quote: Despising one another, they fawn on one another; and wanting to be above one another, they take the lower place beneath one another.
support.follows: People who despise one another fawn on one another, and in wanting to be above one another they put themselves beneath.
gives: I go against myself
I look down on people, yet I fawn on them

support.quote: They are unwilling to speak well of the people who live at the same time as them and alongside them, yet they set great store by being spoken well of themselves by those who come after, whom they have never seen and never will see.
support.follows: It is odd to refuse to speak well of those who live beside me and yet care so much that people I will never see speak well of me.
gives: I go against myself
I will not speak well of those who live beside me, yet I want those who come after to speak well of me

claims.t: Praise does not make me better, and blame does not harm me. Whatever is beautiful is beautiful of itself, and praise is no part of it; my own good is my own action, not another person’s activity.
claims.shared: 4.16 and 9.32 both deny that praise and blame change what they fall on: in 4.16, “what is praised becomes neither worse nor better” and nothing is “ruined when it is blamed”; in 9.32, those who think they “do harm by blaming or do good by singing praises” are conceited.
claims.changed: 4.16 speaks of beautiful things, from law and truth to an emerald; the claim applies it to me. The Greek word for “beautiful” also means fine and noble. 6.46’s “lover of pleasure” is left out.

support.quote: At any rate, what is praised becomes neither worse nor better.
support.follows: Being praised makes a thing neither worse nor better.
gives: Praise does not make me better

support.quote: Which of these is beautiful because it is praised, or is ruined when it is blamed?
support.follows: Nothing is beautiful because it is praised, and nothing is ruined because it is blamed.
gives: Praise does not make me better
blame does not harm me

support.quote: When they suppose that they do harm by blaming or do good by singing praises, how much conceit.
support.follows: People who think their blame does harm, or their praise does good, think far too much of themselves.
gives: Praise does not make me better
blame does not harm me

support.quote: Everything that is beautiful in any way at all is beautiful of itself and ends in itself, and does not have praise as a part of itself.
support.follows: Whatever is beautiful is beautiful of itself, and praise is no part of its beauty.
gives: Whatever is beautiful is beautiful of itself, and praise is no part of it

support.quote: The lover of fame takes their own good to be another person’s activity; the lover of pleasure, their own feeling; the person who has sense, their own action.
support.follows: Whoever loves fame puts their good in what someone else does; a sensible person puts it in their own action.
gives: my own good is my own action, not another person’s activity

single.quote: Then what they are like when lording it and giving themselves airs, or getting angry and scolding from a position of superiority. Yet a little while ago they were slaves, to how many, and for what sort of things. And in a little while they will be in the same sort of case.
single.label: Slaves a little while ago
single.t: When people give themselves airs and scold from above, I remember that a little while ago they were slaves to many, and that in a little while they will be in the same case.
single.why: Only this passage says what the proud were a little while ago and will soon be again. Its first sentence is quoted in claim 1; this part stands alone.
single.follows: Those who give themselves airs and scold from above were slaves to many not long ago, and soon they will be in the same case.

single.quote: But suppose even that those who will remember are immortal, and the memory immortal: what then is that to you? And I do not speak of its being nothing to the dead; but to the living, what is praise, except perhaps for the sake of managing some matter?
single.label: Even if memory lasted
single.t: Even if those who remember me never died, and the memory never died, it would be nothing to me. To the living, praise is of use at most for getting some matter done.
single.why: Only this passage supposes the opposite of what claim 3 rests on, a memory that never dies, and says what holds then.
single.follows: Even an undying memory would be nothing to me; to the living, praise is at most useful for managing some matter.

members.text:
What are their minds and understandings; and what the things that
they apply themselves unto: what do they love, and what do they hate
for? Fancy to thyself the estate of their souls openly to be seen. When
they think they hurt them shrewdly, whom they speak ill of; and when
they think they do them a very good turn, whom they commend and extol: O
how full are they then of conceit, and opinion!
members.english: What the ruling parts of these people are, what sort of things they are in earnest about, and what sort of things win their love and honour. Think of yourself as looking at their little souls naked. When they suppose that they do harm by blaming or do good by singing praises, how much conceit.
members.greek: Τίνα τὰ ἡγεμονικὰ τούτων καὶ περὶ οἷα ἐσπουδάκασι καὶ δι’ οἷα φιλοῦσι καὶ τιμῶσι· γυμνὰ νόμιζε βλέπειν τὰ ψυχάρια αὐτῶν. ὅτε δοκοῦσι βλάπτειν ψέγοντες ἢ ὠφελεῖν ἐξυμνοῦντες, ὅση οἴησις.

members.text:
This time that is now present, bestow thou upon thyself. They that
rather hunt for fame after death, do not consider, that those men that
shall be hereafter, will be even such, as these whom now they can so
hardly bear with. And besides they also will be mortal men. But to
consider the thing in itself, if so many with so many voices, shall make
such and such a sound, or shall have such and such an opinion concerning
thee, what is it to thee?
members.english: Look: make a gift of this present time to yourself. People who instead chase fame after death do not take into account that those people will be others of the same kind as these whom they find hard to bear; and those people too are mortal. And what is it to you at all, if those people echo with sounds of such a kind, or hold a judgment of such a kind about you?
members.greek: Τοῦτον ἰδοὺ τὸν χρόνον σεαυτῷ χάρισαι. οἱ τὴν ὑστεροφημίαν μᾶλλον διώκοντες οὐ λογίζονται ὅτι ἄλλοι τοιοῦτοι μέλλουσιν ἐκεῖνοι εἶναι, οἷοί εἰσιν οὗτοι οὓς βαροῦνται· κἀκεῖνοι δὲ θνητοί. τί δὲ ὅλως πρὸς σέ, ἂν ἐκεῖνοι φωναῖς τοιαύταις ἀπηχῶσιν ἢ ὑπόληψιν τοιαύτην περὶ σοῦ ἔχωσιν;

members.text:
What manner of men they be whom they seek to please, and what to
get, and by what actions: how soon time will cover and bury all things,
and how many it hath already buried!
members.english: What sort of people those are whom they want to please, and for what sort of gains, and through what sort of activities. How quickly eternity will cover everything, and how much it has covered already.
members.greek: Οἷοί εἰσιν οἷς θέλουσιν ἀρέσκειν, καὶ δι’ οἷα περιγινόμενα καὶ δι’ οἵων ἐνεργειῶν. ὡς ταχέως ὁ αἰὼν πάντα καλύψει καὶ ὅσα ἐκάλυψεν ἤδη.

members.text:
He who is greedy of credit and reputation after his death, doth
not consider, that they themselves by whom he is remembered, shall soon
after every one of them be dead; and they likewise that succeed those;
until at last all memory, which hitherto by the succession of men
admiring and soon after dying hath had its course, be quite extinct.
But suppose that both they that shall remember thee, and thy memory
with them should be immortal, what is that to thee? I will not say to
thee after thou art dead; but even to thee living, what is thy praise?
But only for a secret and politic consideration, which we call
οἰκονομίαν, or dispensation. For as for that, that it is the gift of
nature, whatsoever is commended in thee, what might be objected from
thence, let that now that we are upon another consideration be omitted
as unseasonable. That which is fair and goodly, whatsoever it be, and
in what respect soever it be, that it is fair and goodly, it is so of
itself, and terminates in itself, not admitting praise as a part or
member: that therefore which is praised, is not thereby made either
better or worse. This I understand even of those things, that are
commonly called fair and good, as those which are commended either for
the matter itself, or for curious workmanship. As for that which is
truly good, what can it stand in need of more than either justice or
truth; or more than either kindness and modesty? Which of all those,
either becomes good or fair, because commended; or dispraised suffers
any damage? Doth the emerald become worse in itself, or more vile if it
be not commended? Doth gold, or ivory, or purple? Is there anything
that doth though never so common, as a knife, a flower, or a tree?
members.english:
Whoever is worked up about fame after death does not picture that each of those who remember them will very soon die too; then in turn the one who takes over from that one, until the whole memory also goes out, as it passes on through those that are lit and go out. But suppose even that those who will remember are immortal, and the memory immortal: what then is that to you? And I do not speak of its being nothing to the dead; but to the living, what is praise, except perhaps for the sake of managing some matter? For leave aside now, out of season, the gift of nature, which from here on belongs to some other discussion.

Everything that is beautiful in any way at all is beautiful of itself and ends in itself, and does not have praise as a part of itself. At any rate, what is praised becomes neither worse nor better. I say this also of the things called beautiful in the more ordinary way, such as material things and things made by craft (for what does the truly beautiful need? No more than law does, no more than truth, no more than goodwill or a sense of shame). Which of these is beautiful because it is praised, or is ruined when it is blamed? For does a little emerald become worse than itself if it is not praised? And what of gold, ivory, purple, a lyre, a small knife, a little flower, a little tree?
members.greek:
Ὁ περὶ τὴν ὑστεροφημίαν ἐπτοημένος οὐ φαντάζεται ὅτι ἕκαστος τῶν μεμνημένων αὐτοῦ τάχιστα καὶ αὐτὸς ἀποθανεῖται· εἶτα πάλιν ὁ ἐκεῖνον διαδεξάμενος, μέχρι καὶ πᾶσα ἡ μνήμη ἀποσβῇ διὰ ἁπτομένων καὶ σβεννυμένων προιοῦσα. ὑπόθου δ᾽, ὅτι καὶ ἀθάνατοι μὲν οἱ μεμνησόμενοι, ἀθάνατος δὲ ἡ μνήμη· τί οὖν τοῦτο πρὸς σέ; καὶ οὐ λέγω, ὅτι οὐδὲν πρὸς τὸν τεθνηκότα, ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὸν ζῶντα τί ὁ ἔπαινος, πλὴν ἄρα δι’ οἰκονομίαν τινά; πάρες γὰρ νῦν ἀκαίρως τὴν φυσικὴν δόσιν ἄλλου τινὸς ἐχομένην λόγου λοιπόν.

Πᾶν τὸ καὶ ὁπωσοῦν καλὸν ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ καλόν ἐστι καὶ ἐφ’ ἑαυτὸ καταλήγει, οὐκ ἔχον μέρος ἑαυτοῦ τὸν ἔπαινον· οὔτε γοῦν χεῖρον ἣ κρεῖττον γίνεται τὸ ἐπαινούμενον. τοῦτό φημι καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν κοινότερον καλῶν λεγομένων, οἷον ἐπὶ τῶν ὑλικῶν καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν τεχνικῶν κατασκευασμάτων (τὸ γὰρ δὴ ὄντως καλὸν τίνος χρείαν ἔχει; οὐ μᾶλλον ἣ νόμος, οὐ μᾶλλον ἣ ἀλήθεια, οὐ μᾶλλον ἢ εὔνοια ἢ αἰδώς)· τί τούτων διὰ τὸ ἐπαινεῖσθαι καλόν ἐστιν ἢ ψεγόμενον φθείρεται; σμαράγδιον γὰρ ἑαυτοῦ χεῖρον γίνεται, ἐὰν μὴ ἐπαινῆται; τί δὲ χρυσός, ἐλέφας, πορφύρα, λύρα, μαχαίριον, ἀνθύλλιον, δενδρύφιον;

members.text:
Who can choose but wonder at them? They will not speak well of
them that are at the same time with them, and live with them; yet they
themselves are very ambitious, that they that shall follow, whom they
have never seen, nor shall ever see, should speak well of them. As if
a man should grieve that he hath not been commended by them, that lived
before him.
members.english: What a thing they do. They are unwilling to speak well of the people who live at the same time as them and alongside them, yet they set great store by being spoken well of themselves by those who come after, whom they have never seen and never will see. This is almost as if you were pained that those who came before did not also speak well of you.
members.greek: Οἷόν ἐστιν ὃ ποιοῦσι. τοὺς μὲν ἐπὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ χρόνου καὶ μεθ’ ἑαυτῶν ζῶντας ἀνθρώπους εὐφημεῖν οὐ θέλουσιν, αὐτοὶ δὲ ὑπὸ τῶν μεταγενεστέρων εὐφημηθῆναι, οὓς οὔτε εἶδόν ποτε οὔτε ὄψονται, περὶ πολλοῦ ποιοῦνται. τοῦτο δὲ ἐγγύς ἐστι τῷ λυπηθῆναι ἄν, ὅτι οὐχὶ καὶ οἱ προγενέστεροι περὶ σοῦ λόγους εὐφήμους ἐποιοῦντο.

members.text:
He that knoweth not what the world is, knoweth not where he himself
is. And he that knoweth not what the world was made for, cannot possibly
know either what are the qualities, or what is the nature of the world.
Now he that in either of these is to seek, for what he himself was made
is ignorant also. What then dost thou think of that man, who proposeth
unto himself, as a matter of great moment, the noise and applause
of men, who both where they are, and what they are themselves, are
altogether ignorant? Dost thou desire to be commended of that man, who
thrice in one hour perchance, doth himself curse himself? Dost thou
desire to please him, who pleaseth not himself? or dost thou think that
he pleaseth himself, who doth use to repent himself almost of everything
that he doth?
members.english:
Whoever does not know what the universe is does not know where they are. Whoever does not know what it is by nature for does not know who they are, nor what the universe is. And whoever is missing any one of these could not even say what they themselves are by nature for. What, then, does a person seem to you to be who runs from or chases the praise of those who clap, people who know neither where they are nor who they are?

Do you want to be praised by a person who curses themselves three times an hour? Do you want to please a person who is not pleased with themselves? Is a person pleased with themselves who regrets nearly everything they do?
members.greek:
Ὁ μὲν μὴ εἰδὼς ὅ τι ἐστὶ κόσμος, οὐκ οἶδεν ὅπου ἐστίν. ὁ δὲ μὴ εἰδὼς πρὸς ὅ τι πέφυκεν, οὐκ οἶδεν ὅστις ἐστὶν οὐδὲ τί ἐστι κόσμος. ὁ δὲ ἕν τι τούτων ἀπολιπὼν οὐδὲ πρὸς ὅ τι αὐτὸς πέφυκεν εἴποι. τίς οὖν φαίνεταί σοι ὁ τὸν τῶν κροτούντων ἔπαινον φεύγων ἢ διώκων, οἳ οὔθ’ ὅπου εἰσὶν οὔτε οἵτινές εἰσι γινώσκουσιν;

Ἐπαινεῖσθαι θέλεις ὑπὸ ἀνθρώπου τρὶς τῆς ὥρας ἑαυτῷ καταρωμένου; ἀρέσκειν θέλεις ἀνθρώπῳ ὃς οὐκ ἀρέσκει ἑαυτῷ; ἀρέσκει ἑαυτῷ ὁ μετανοῶν ἐφ’ ἅπασι σχεδὸν οἷς πράσσει;

members.text:
Consider them through all actions and occupations, of their lives:
as when they eat, and when they sleep: when they are in the act of
necessary exoneration, and when in the act of lust. Again, when they
either are in their greatest exultation; and in the middle of all
their pomp and glory; or being angry and displeased, in great state and
majesty, as from an higher place, they chide and rebuke. How base and
slavish, but a little while ago, they were fain to be, that they might
come to this; and within a very little while what will be their estate,
when death hath once seized upon them.
members.english: What they are like when eating, sleeping, mating, emptying their bowels, and the rest. Then what they are like when lording it and giving themselves airs, or getting angry and scolding from a position of superiority. Yet a little while ago they were slaves, to how many, and for what sort of things. And in a little while they will be in the same sort of case.
members.greek: Οἷοί εἰσιν ἐσθίοντες, καθεύδοντες, ὀχεύοντες, ἀποπατοῦντες, τὰ ἄλλα· εἶτα οἷοι ἀνδρονομούμενοι καὶ γαυρούμενοι ἢ χαλεπαίνοντες καὶ ἐξ ὑπεροχῆς ἐπιπλήττοντες, πρὸ ὀλίγου δὲ ἐδούλευον πόσοις καὶ δι’ οἷα· καὶ μετ’ ὀλίγον ἐν τοιούτοις ἔσονται.

members.text:
I have often wondered how it should come to pass, that every man
loving himself best, should more regard other men's opinions concerning
himself than his own. For if any God or grave master standing by,
should command any of us to think nothing by himself but what he should
presently speak out; no man were able to endure it, though but for one
day. Thus do we fear more what our neighbours will think of us, than
what we ourselves.
members.english: I have often wondered how it is that each person loves themselves more than everyone else, yet sets less value on their own judgment about themselves than on that of others. At any rate, if a god appears beside someone, or a sensible teacher, and tells them to turn over nothing in their mind and think nothing to themselves that they will not at the same moment bring out, crying it aloud, they will not put up with this for even one day. So it is that we feel more shame before those near us, at what they will think of us, than before ourselves.
members.greek: Πολλάκις ἐθαύμασα πῶς ἑαυτὸν μὲν ἕκαστος μᾶλλον πάντων φιλεῖ, τὴν δὲ ἑαυτοῦ περὶ αὑτοῦ ὑπόληψιν ἐν ἐλάττονι λόγῳ τίθεται ἢ τὴν τῶν ἄλλων. ἐὰν γοῦν τινα θεὸς ἐπιστὰς ἢ διδάσκαλος ἔμφρων κελεύσῃ μηδὲν καθ’ ἑαυτὸν ἐνθυμεῖσθαι καὶ διανοεῖσθαι ὃ μὴ ἄμα καὶ γεγωνίσκων ἐξοίσει, οὐδὲ πρὸς μίαν ἡμέραν τοῦτο ὑπομενεῖ. οὕτως τοὺς πέλας μᾶλλον αἰδούμεθα, τί ποτε περὶ ἡμῶν φρονήσουσιν, ἢ ἑαυτούς.

members.text:
Behold and observe, what is the state of their rational part; and
those that the world doth account wise, see what things they fly and are
afraid of; and what things they hunt after.
members.english: Look closely into their ruling parts, and at the wise as well: what sort of things they run from, and what sort of things they chase.
members.greek: Τὰ ἡγεμονικὰ αὐτῶν διάβλεπε καὶ τοὺς φρονίμους, οἷα μὲν φεύγουσιν, οἷα δὲ διώκουσιν.

members.text:
Sift their minds and understandings, and behold what men they be,
whom thou dost stand in fear of what they shall judge of thee, what they
themselves judge of themselves.
members.english: Pass inside, right inside, into their ruling parts, and you will see what judges you are afraid of, and what sort of judges they are of themselves as well.
members.greek: Δίελθε ἔσω ἔσω εἰς τὰ ἡγεμονικὰ αὐτῶν καὶ ὄψει τίνας κριτὰς φοβῇ, οἵους καὶ περὶ αὑτῶν ὄντας κριτάς.

members.text:
They contemn one another, and yet they seek to please one another:
and whilest they seek to surpass one another in worldly pomp and
greatness, they most debase and prostitute themselves in their better
part one to another.
members.english: Despising one another, they fawn on one another; and wanting to be above one another, they take the lower place beneath one another.
members.greek: Ἀλλήλων καταφρονοῦντες ἀλλήλοις ἀρεσκεύονται καὶ ἀλλήλων ὑπερέχειν θέλοντες ἀλλήλοις ὑποκατακλίνονται.

members.text:
The ambitious supposeth another man's act, praise and applause, to
be his own happiness; the voluptuous his own sense and feeling; but he
that is wise, his own action.
members.english: The lover of fame takes their own good to be another person’s activity; the lover of pleasure, their own feeling; the person who has sense, their own action.
members.greek: Ὁ μὲν φιλόδοξος ἀλλοτρίαν ἐνέργειαν ἴδιον ἀγαθὸν ὑπολαμβάνει, ὁ δὲ φιλήδονος ἰδίαν πεῖσιν, ὁ δὲ νοῦν ἔχων ἰδίαν πρᾶξιν.

members.why: About pride in a capture, from a spider’s fly to the Sarmatians Marcus himself fought. It shares with claim 1 the act of examining people’s principles, but turns it on pride in conquest, not on those whose praise or judgment I care about.
members.text:
As the spider, when it hath caught the fly that it hunted after, is
not little proud, nor meanly conceited of herself: as he likewise that
hath caught an hare, or hath taken a fish with his net: as another for
the taking of a boar, and another of a bear: so may they be proud,
and applaud themselves for their valiant acts against the Sarmatai, or
northern nations lately defeated. For these also, these famous soldiers
and warlike men, if thou dost look into their minds and opinions, what
do they for the most part but hunt after prey?
members.english: A little spider thinks a great deal of itself for having hunted down a fly; someone else for a little hare, another for a sprat in a hand net, another for little boars, another for bears, another for Sarmatians. For are these not robbers, if you examine their principles?
members.greek: Ἀράχνιον μυῖαν θηρᾶσαν μέγα φρονεῖ, ἄλλος δὲ λαγίδιον, ἄλλος δὲ ὑποχῇ ἀφύην, ἄλλος δὲ συίδια, ἄλλος δὲ ἄρκτους, ἄλλος Σαρμάτας. οὗτοι γὰρ οὐ λῃσταί, ἐὰν τὰ δόγματα ἐξετάζῃς;

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 9.32 is 9.34, 8.42 is 8.44, 6.54 is 6.59, 4.16 is 4.19–20, 6.17 is 6.18, 8.51 is 8.52–53, 10.20 is 10.19, 12.3 is 12.4, 4.31 is 4.38, 9.16 is 9.18, 11.13 is 11.14 and 6.46 is 6.51; 10.10 is the same.

Reads 9.16’s “what sort of judges they are of themselves” as poor judges of themselves. The Greek says only “what sort”; the poor judgment is the sense of the context and is said outright in 8.51, which claim 2 joins to it.

Applies to me what the passages say of others: 4.16 of beautiful things (“what is praised becomes neither worse nor better”), and 12.3, 11.13 and 6.17 of “each person” and “they”. In claim 4, all three are mapped to “I go against myself”, the editor’s own name for the contradiction each shows.
Sets aside 10.10, the spider proud of its fly. It is about pride in a capture, not about anyone’s praise or judgment.
articles.limit: Article 22 already says that I fail when I want to be approved of, Article 10 that being remembered is of no account, Article 13 that praise from the many pulls me about, and Article 9 that I need no one as witness. Article 34 already says that those who remember me will soon follow me and that even remembrance lasting for ever would be empty; claim 3 and the item under “If I doubt it” say this again, here as reasons not to chase fame after death. What this article adds is the reason from the side of the people who give praise: I look into them and find poor judges, even of themselves; praise and blame do not change what they fall on; and those who would remember me will be people like the ones I find hard to bear now (8.42). 4.16 carries much of it: it is quoted in claims 3 and 5 and in the item under “If I doubt it”, and two parts of the statement rest on it.

articles.title: Wrongdoing harms the wrongdoer

statement.t: A wrong harms the one who does it, not the one it is done to, so I leave another’s wrong with them.

parts.words: A wrong harms the one who does it, not the one it is done to
I leave another’s wrong with them

inferences.why: No passage joins the two. 9.18 says to leave another’s wrong there without giving a reason; the step from where the harm lies to leaving the wrong with its doer is the editor’s.

statement.kind: A ground and the response it allows
statement.form: Claim 1 is the ground: the harm of a wrong lies with the one who does it. Claim 2 is what I do when the wrong is someone else’s: I count it no evil for me and leave it with them. The “so” that joins them in the statement is the editor’s. In the part “I leave another’s wrong with them”, 8.53 supports only the words “another’s wrong”; the leaving comes from 9.18.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, where the harm of a wrong lies gains a second author and a challenge: he holds that the smallest and lightest part of a wrong reaches the one it is done to, and that bad people make one another worse. Practice gains forgetting wrongs on purpose and reading words and looks kindly, and In action gains keeping watch against what people may do.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands, except that its middle, that a wrong does no harm to the one it is done to, is challenged under Why: he holds that its smallest and lightest part reaches them. It also gains an ending: I forget another’s wrong on purpose.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: the first and greatest punishment of those who do wrong is to have done wrong
piece.follows: The first and greatest punishment of wrongdoing is having done it.
piece.context: Letter 97, on the wickedness of the age: Seneca agrees with Epicurus that wrongdoers never feel safe. The first punishment of wrongdoing falls on the one who did it.
gives: The evil of a wrong lies with the one who does it

items.label: practice
items.t: I think little of the wrongs done to me and forget them, not through carelessness but on purpose. I do not put a bad meaning on words or looks, and I lighten whatever happens by reading it kindly.
items.why: In this section Marcus says to leave another’s wrong where it is, and that perhaps no wrong was done; he gives no exercise for it. Seneca gives one: forget wrongs on purpose, and read words and looks kindly.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: He scorns the things that have hurt him, and he forgets not through carelessness but by choice.
support.follows: The wise man thinks little of the wrongs done to him and forgets them on purpose.
support.context: Letter 81, on benefits: the wise man takes lasting joy in what he has received. “He” is the wise man; “the things that have hurt him” are injuries other people have done him.
gives: I think little of the wrongs done to me
forget them, not through carelessness but on purpose

support.author: seneca
support.quote: He does not put a bad meaning on words or looks; whatever happens, he lightens it by interpreting it kindly.
support.follows: The wise man does not put a bad meaning on words or looks, and lightens whatever happens by reading it kindly.
support.context: Letter 81, on weighing injuries against benefits. “He” is the wise man, who does not look for someone to blame and puts people’s wrongdoings down to fortune.
gives: I do not put a bad meaning on words or looks
I lighten whatever happens by reading it kindly

items.label: action
items.role: Guarding my life and goods against people
items.t: Other people are where my daily danger comes from. I watch for it so that I am not harmed, and I keep my duty to people in view so that I do not harm them.
items.why: Seneca means danger to life and goods, which he sets beside fires and falling buildings, not an evil for the mind. Marcus says what another’s wrong is once it has been done; nothing in this section says to guard against it beforehand.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: from man to man the danger is daily. Make yourself ready against this, and keep your eyes fixed on this.
support.follows: A person’s daily danger comes from other people, so one should make oneself ready against it and keep one’s eyes fixed on it.
support.context: Letter 103, on the dangers of living among people. Seneca sets plots by people against accidents such as fires and falling buildings; “this” is the danger from people.
gives: Other people are where my daily danger comes from
I watch for it

support.author: seneca
support.quote: think about what danger comes from man in such a way that you think about what the duty of man is. Keep your eyes on the one so that you are not harmed, on the other so that you do not harm.
support.follows: One should keep the danger from people in view so as not to be harmed, and the duty of a person in view so as not to harm.
support.context: Letter 103: from the danger people pose, Seneca draws a duty. Here “harmed” means hurt by others in life and goods, the danger the letter opens with.
gives: I keep my duty to people in view so that I do not harm them

items.t: Seneca agrees that the worst of a wrong stays with the one who does it, but he holds that some of it reaches the other person: the “smallest and lightest part of wickedness spills over onto others” (Ep. 81.22). He also says that bad people harm one another, each making the other worse (Ep. 109.4). Marcus says that a particular wickedness does no harm to the other person at all.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The smallest and lightest part of wickedness spills over onto others: what is worst in it and, so to speak, thickest stays at home and presses on the one who has it
support.follows: Of our wickedness, only the smallest part spills over onto others; the worst part stays with us and presses on us.
support.context: Letter 81, on benefits: Seneca says to avoid ingratitude for our own sake. By “wickedness” he means the wrong we do; the “others” are those it is done to, here the benefactor.

passages.title: On vice in every age and the guilty conscience
passages.text: I do not judge that this conflicts with our school, if it is explained in this way. Why? Because the first and greatest punishment of those who do wrong is to have done wrong, and no crime, even if Fortune adorns it with her gifts, even if she protects and defends it, is unpunished, since the penalty of crime is in the crime. But nonetheless these second punishments too press hard upon that first one and follow it: always to be afraid, to take fright, and to have no trust in one’s own security. Why should I free wickedness from this penalty? Why should I not leave it always in suspense?

passages.title: On gratitude and repaying favours
passages.text: Bad men have one pleasure, and that a short one, while they are receiving benefits; from those benefits a long joy, one that does not fail, stays with the wise man. For what delights him is not receiving but having received, which is undying and constant. He scorns the things that have hurt him, and he forgets not through carelessness but by choice.

passages.title: On gratitude and repaying favours
passages.text: He does not turn everything to the worse, nor does he look for someone to blame for an accident, and he puts men’s wrongdoings down to fortune instead. He does not put a bad meaning on words or looks; whatever happens, he lightens it by interpreting it kindly. He does not remember an offence rather than a service. As far as he can he keeps to the earlier and better memory, and his mind does not change towards those who have done well by him unless the bad deeds far outstrip the good and the difference is plain even to one who shuts his eyes; and even then only this far, that after the greater wrong he is as he was before the benefit. For when the wrong is equal to the benefit, some goodwill remains in the mind.

passages.title: On the danger people pose to each other
passages.text: Why do you look about for those things that can perhaps happen to you but can also not happen? I mean fire, the collapse of a building, other things that fall on us but do not lie in wait for us. Look rather at those, avoid those: the things that watch us, that try to catch us. Being shipwrecked, being overturned in a carriage: these are rare accidents, even if serious ones; from man to man the danger is daily. Make yourself ready against this, and keep your eyes fixed on this. No evil is more frequent, none more persistent, none more ingratiating.

passages.title: On the danger people pose to each other
passages.text: For your part, however, think about what danger comes from man in such a way that you think about what the duty of man is. Keep your eyes on the one so that you are not harmed, on the other so that you do not harm. Be glad when things go well for anyone, be moved when they go badly, and remember what you ought to fulfil and what you ought to guard against.

passages.title: On gratitude and repaying favours
passages.text: So let us avoid being ungrateful, not for another’s sake but for our own. The smallest and lightest part of wickedness spills over onto others: what is worst in it and, so to speak, thickest stays at home and presses on the one who has it, as our Attalus used to say: “Vice itself drinks the greatest part of its own poison.” That poison which snakes bring out to destroy others, and hold without destroying themselves, is not like this one: this one is worst for those who have it.

passages.title: On whether the wise can help the wise
passages.text: A bad man harms a bad man and makes him worse, by stirring up his anger, by going along with his gloom, by praising his pleasures; and bad men suffer most when they have mixed their vices most and their wickedness has been brought together into one. So, conversely, a good man will benefit a good man. “How?” you say.

claims.role: Where the harm of a wrong lies
claims.t: The evil of a wrong lies with the one who does it: it harms them and makes them bad, and they can be rid of it as soon as they wish. It does no harm to the person it is done to.

single.quote: To my faculty of choice, my neighbour’s faculty of choice is just as much a matter of indifference as their bit of breath and their bit of flesh. For however true it is that we have come to be for one another’s sake, still each of our ruling parts has its own authority.
single.label: Each mind rules itself
single.t: Another person’s power of choice is neither good nor bad for mine, any more than their breath or their flesh. We were made for one another, but each of us has a ruling mind with its own authority.
single.why: Only 8.53 says why another person’s wrong cannot reach me: each ruling part has its own authority.
single.follows: My neighbour’s power of choice is neither good nor bad for mine; though we exist for one another, each mind has its own authority.

single.quote: But perhaps they did not do wrong.
single.label: Perhaps no wrong
single.t: When I think someone has done wrong, I also allow that perhaps they did not.
single.why: Only 9.37 doubts that the wrong was done at all. It is a check before the claim applies, not a part of it.
single.follows: It may be that the person did not do wrong at all.

single.quote: What is wickedness? This is what you have often seen. And with everything that happens, keep this at hand: this is what you have often seen.
single.label: Nothing new
single.t: When I meet wickedness, and whatever else happens, I keep this thought ready: this is what I have often seen.
single.why: Only 7.1 gives words to keep ready when wickedness is met. It speaks of how familiar wickedness is, not of whom it harms.
single.follows: Wickedness is what one has often seen, and the same thought is to be kept at hand for whatever happens.

single.quote: the wrong done with pleasure is open to a greater charge than the wrong done with pain. And in general the one is more like a person who has first been treated unjustly and has been forced by pain into anger; the other is moved to do injustice by an impulse of their own, carried towards doing something from desire.
single.label: Wrong done for pleasure
single.t: Of the wrongs I might do, one done with pleasure is worse than one done in the pain of anger. In anger I am more like someone wronged first and forced by pain into anger; from desire I go to the wrong by an impulse of my own.
single.why: Only 2.7 compares wrongs, and it reports Theophrastus with Marcus’s approval. It is about how serious a wrong is, not whom it harms, and it shows what my own failing looks like.
single.follows: Theophrastus, whom Marcus approves, holds that a wrong done with pleasure deserves a greater charge than a wrong done in the pain of anger.

single.quote: Often the one who does not do something acts unjustly, not only the one who does something.
single.label: Wrong by not acting
single.t: I can act unjustly by not doing something, and not only by doing something.
single.why: Only 9.4 speaks of a wrong done by leaving something undone. It widens what counts as my wrong.
single.follows: Leaving something undone can be unjust, as well as doing something.

members.text:
Wickedness in general doth not hurt the world. Particular
wickedness doth not hurt any other: only unto him it is hurtful,
whosoever he be that offends, unto whom in great favour and mercy it is
granted, that whensoever he himself shall but first desire it, he may be
presently delivered of it. Unto my free-will my neighbour's free-will,
whoever he be, (as his life, or his bode), is altogether indifferent.
For though we are all made one for another, yet have our minds and
understandings each of them their own proper and limited jurisdiction.
For else another man's wickedness might be my evil which God would not
have, that it might not be in another man's power to make me unhappy:
which nothing now can do but mine own wickedness.
members.english:
Wickedness in general does no harm to the universe, and wickedness in the particular case does no harm to the other person. It is harmful only to the one who has also been given the power to be rid of it, as soon as they wish to.

To my faculty of choice, my neighbour’s faculty of choice is just as much a matter of indifference as their bit of breath and their bit of flesh. For however true it is that we have come to be for one another’s sake, still each of our ruling parts has its own authority. Otherwise my neighbour’s wickedness would be an evil for me, which god decided against, so that my being unfortunate should not depend on someone else.

members.text:
Theophrastus, where he compares sin with sin (as after a vulgar
sense such things I grant may be compared:) says well and like a
philosopher, that those sins are greater which are committed through
lust, than those which are committed through anger. For he that is angry
seems with a kind of grief and close contraction of himself, to turn
away from reason; but he that sins through lust, being overcome by
pleasure, doth in his very sin bewray a more impotent, and unmanlike
disposition. Well then and like a philosopher doth he say, that he of
the two is the more to be condemned, that sins with pleasure, than he
that sins with grief. For indeed this latter may seem first to have been
wronged, and so in some manner through grief thereof to have been forced
to be angry, whereas he who through lust doth commit anything, did of
himself merely resolve upon that action.
members.english: Theophrastus speaks as a philosopher when, in his comparison of wrongdoings (as one might compare such things in a more everyday way), he says that offences committed from desire are more serious than those committed from anger. For the one who is angry is seen to turn away from reason with a certain pain and a shrinking inside that goes unnoticed; but the one who does wrong from desire, overcome by pleasure, is seen to be somehow more unrestrained and more womanish in their wrongdoing. Rightly, then, and in a way worthy of philosophy, he said that the wrong done with pleasure is open to a greater charge than the wrong done with pain. And in general the one is more like a person who has first been treated unjustly and has been forced by pain into anger; the other is moved to do injustice by an impulse of their own, carried towards doing something from desire.
members.greek: Φιλοσόφως ὁ Θεόφραστος ἐν τῇ συγκρίσει τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων, ὡς ἄν τις κοινότερον τὰ τοιαῦτα συγκρίνειε, φησὶ βαρύτερα εἶναι τὰ κατ’ ἐπιθυμίαν πλημμελούμενα τῶν κατὰ θυμόν. ὁ γὰρ θυμούμενος μετά τινος λύπης καὶ λεληθυίας συστολῆς φαίνεται τὸν λόγον ἀποστρεφόμενος· ὁ δὲ κατ’ ἐπιθυμίαν ἁμαρτάνων, ὑφ’ ἡδονῆς ἡττώμενος ἀκολαστότερός πως φαίνεται καὶ θηλύτερος ἐν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις. ὀρθῶς οὖν καὶ φιλοσοφίας ἀξίως ἔφη μείζονος ἐγκλήματος ἔχεσθαι τὸ μεθ’ ἡδονῆς ἁμαρτανόμενον ἤπερ τὸ μετὰ λύπης· ὅλως τε ὁ μὲν προηδικημένῳ μᾶλλον ἔοικε καὶ διὰ λύπης ἠναγκασμένῳ θυμωθῆναι· ὁ δὲ αὐτόθεν πρὸς τὸ ἀδικεῖν ὥρμηται, φερόμενος ἐπὶ τὸ πρᾶξαί τι κατ’ ἐπιθυμίαν.

members.why: About regret: it argues that pleasure is neither useful nor good. It says nothing about wrongdoing or about whom a wrong harms.
members.text:
Repentance is an inward and self-reprehension for the neglect or
omission of somewhat that was profitable. Now whatsoever is good, is
also profitable, and it is the part of an honest virtuous man to set by
it, and to make reckoning of it accordingly. But never did any honest
virtuous man repent of the neglect or omission of any carnal pleasure:
no carnal pleasure then is either good or profitable.
members.english: Regret is a kind of reproach against oneself for having let something useful go by. But what is useful must be something good, and the honourable and good man must attend to it. And no honourable and good man would regret having let a pleasure go by. So pleasure is neither useful nor good.

members.text:
What is wickedness? It is that which many time and often thou hast
already seen and known in the world. And so oft as anything doth happen
that might otherwise trouble thee, let this memento presently come to
thy mind, that it is that which thou hast already often Seen and known.
Generally, above and below, thou shalt find but the same things. The
very same things whereof ancient stories, middle age stories, and fresh
stories are full whereof towns are full, and houses full. There is
nothing that is new. All things that are, are both usual and of little
continuance.
members.english: What is wickedness? This is what you have often seen. And with everything that happens, keep this at hand: this is what you have often seen. In general, high and low, you will find the same things. The histories are full of them, the ancient ones, those in between and the recent ones; cities and households are full of them now. Nothing is new. Everything is both familiar and short-lived.
members.greek: Τί ἐστι κακία; τοῦτ’ ἔστιν ὃ πολλάκις εἶδες. καὶ ἐπὶ παντὸς δὲ τοῦ συμβαίνοντος πρόχειρον ἔχε ὅτι τοῦτό ἐστιν ὃ πολλάκις εἶδες. ὅλως ἄνω κάτω τὰ αὐτὰ εὑρήσεις, ὧν μεσταὶ αἱ ἱστορίαι αἱ παλαιαί, αἱ μέσαι, αἱ ὑπόγυιοι· ὧν νῦν μεσταὶ αἱ πόλεις καὶ αἱ οἰκίαι. οὐδὲν καινόν· πάντα καὶ συνήθη καὶ ὀλιγοχρόνια.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 8.53 is 8.55–56, 9.4 is 9.4–5, 2.7 is 2.10, 9.18 is 9.20, 9.37 is 9.38 and 8.9 is 8.10; 7.1 is the same.
Treats wickedness (8.53), doing wrong and acting unjustly (9.4), and wrongdoing (9.18, 9.37) as one thing, “a wrong”. The Greek uses three different words for them.
Reads “there” in 9.18 and 9.37 as “with the one who did the wrong”, as the translators’ notes do. The Greek says only “there”.
Keeps 2.7 as a said-once item under “When it breaks”. It reports Theophrastus’s ranking of wrongs with Marcus’s approval, and Marcus says that such a comparison is an everyday way of speaking.
articles.limit: Article 19’s claim 2 is this article’s claim 1, and both articles mark Ep. 81.22 as a challenge to it, because Seneca lets the least part of a wrong reach the one wronged; Article 19’s claim 8 is the said-once 9.37b. What this article adds is leaving the wrong with the one who did it, which Article 21 says once (7.21b) and which here rests on 8.53 and 9.18, with the reason that another’s wrong is no evil for me. The articles disagree about the wrongdoer: Article 19’s claim 1 says that with their disposition they can do nothing else, while claim 1 here says they can be rid of the wrong as soon as they wish, as Article 15’s claim 4 says of my own wrong, and 2.7 calls a wrong done from desire an impulse of one’s own. The two claims rest on four passages, two of them one-line sayings; Article 1 (cutting myself off by wrongdoing) and Article 3 (nothing is unusual) come near.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the article gains what Marcus leaves out here: a fall from a height has no evil in it; a wise person’s good is shared with the people they live with; the worst part of wickedness stays with the one who has it; a person’s good is a free mind, standing tall and under none; a spiteful companion rubs off on me; and I should not become like the bad because they are many. The article has no claims, only said-once items, so he backs none and limits nothing.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains one clause: my good is a free mind, standing tall, that puts itself under none.

items.label: why
items.role: A fall has no evil in it
items.t: A fall from a high place in life has no evil in it, if I look to the end: past death, nature throws no one down.
items.why: 9.15 says that for a thrown stone, coming down is nothing bad, and does not say what the stone stands for. Seneca says it of a person who falls from prosperity, and gives his reason: death is the lowest point. This stands beside the stone, not as the statement’s ground.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: But that falling itself has no evil in it, if you look to the end, beyond which nature has thrown no one down.
support.follows: A fall from a height has no evil in it for one who looks to the end, beyond which nature throws no one down.
support.context: Letter 110: Seneca has just said that privileges often only raise people to a height they then fall from. Here “that falling itself” is the fall from that height; “the end” is death.

items.label: why
items.t: If I am wise, my good is a shared good: it is the good of the people I live with, and my own as well.
items.why: 6.49 says that what is not good for the hive is not good for the bee. Seneca says something near it, but not the same: the wise man’s own good is shared with the people he lives with. 6.49 speaks of advantage, Seneca of the good. This stands beside the hive, not as the statement’s ground.

support.quote: [The wise man’s] is a shared good: it is both the good of those he lives with and his own.

support.context: Letter 85: a helmsman’s art serves only those he carries, but the wise man’s good, his wisdom, serves the people around him and himself alike.

items.label: why
items.role: The worst of wickedness stays at home
items.t: Only the smallest part of my wickedness spills over onto others; the worst part stays with me and presses on me.
items.why: 6.5 says the best way to fight back is not to become like those I fight, and gives no reason. Seneca gives a reason that fits, if “become like them” means doing wrong in return (the editor’s reading, not Marcus’s): wickedness harms the one who has it most. He says it of ingratitude, not of fighting back.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The smallest and lightest part of wickedness spills over onto others: what is worst in it and, so to speak, thickest stays at home and presses on the one who has it
support.follows: The worst part of wickedness stays with the one who has it, not with those it spills over onto.
support.context: Letter 81, on benefits: Seneca urges Lucilius not to be ungrateful, for his own sake. Here “it” is wickedness, and ingratitude is his example.

items.label: why
items.t: A person’s good is a free mind, standing tall, which puts other things under itself and itself under none.
items.why: 7.9 says to be upright, not held upright. Seneca asks what a person’s good is and answers: a free mind, standing tall, under none. He does not define uprightness; he names standing tall as one mark of that good.

support.quote: a free mind, standing tall, putting other things under itself and itself under none
support.follows: A person’s good is a free mind that stands tall, rules other things and is ruled by none.
support.context: Letter 124, on the true good: the quote answers “what is this good?”, meaning a person’s own good, which exists only when reason is perfected, and which few reach even in old age.

items.t: A spiteful companion rubs off on me, even when I am clean. I should not become like the bad because they are many.
items.why: 6.5 says not to become like those I fight, and does not say how that happens. Seneca shows one way it happens, through company; he says it of companions and the crowd, not of people one is fighting.

support.context: Letter 7, on crowds: Seneca warns Lucilius that company shapes character. Here “a man” is anyone, however clean, who keeps a spiteful companion.

passages.title: On empty fears and true riches
passages.text: But that falling itself has no evil in it, if you look to the end, beyond which nature has thrown no one down. The limit of all things is near; near, I say, is both that from which the fortunate man is thrown out and that from which the unfortunate man is let go: we stretch both out and make them long by hope and fear. But, if you are wise, measure all things by the human condition; draw in together both what you rejoice at and what you fear. And it is worth the price to rejoice at nothing for long, so that you may not fear anything for long.

passages.title: On rejecting even moderate passions
passages.text: Next, the helmsman’s art is a good that belongs to others: it is for those he carries, as the doctor’s is for those he treats. [The wise man’s] is a shared good: it is both the good of those he lives with and his own. And so the helmsman, whose service, promised to others, is hindered by a storm, may perhaps be harmed.

passages.title: On gratitude and repaying favours
passages.text: So let us avoid being ungrateful, not for another’s sake but for our own. The smallest and lightest part of wickedness spills over onto others: what is worst in it and, so to speak, thickest stays at home and presses on the one who has it, as our Attalus used to say: “Vice itself drinks the greatest part of its own poison.” That poison which snakes bring out to destroy others, and hold without destroying themselves, is not like this one: this one is worst for those who have it.

passages.title: On the good belonging to reason alone
passages.text: But what is this good? I will tell you: a free mind, standing tall, putting other things under itself and itself under none. Infancy is so far from being able to take in this good that boyhood does not hope for it and youth hopes for it presumptuously; old age is doing well if it has reached it by long and concentrated effort. If this is the good, it is also a thing grasped by the understanding.

passages.title: On avoiding the crowd
passages.text: A single example of luxury or of greed does a great deal of harm: a self-indulgent housemate little by little weakens and softens, a rich neighbour stirs up craving, a spiteful companion rubs his own rust off on a man however spotless and straightforward. What do you think happens to a character that has come under attack from the people as a body?

passages.title: On avoiding the crowd
passages.text: You are bound either to imitate or to hate. But both are to be avoided: do not become like the bad because they are many, and do not become an enemy to many because they are unlike you. Withdraw into yourself as far as you can; keep company with those who will make you better, and let in those whom you in your turn can make better. This works both ways, and people learn while they teach.

single.quote: For a stone that has been thrown upward, it is nothing bad to be carried down, and nothing good to be carried up.
single.label: Up or down
single.t: For a stone thrown upward, coming down is nothing bad, and going up is nothing good.
single.why: Only this passage of the section speaks of what is good or bad in what happens to a thing. It is an image, and Marcus does not say here what the stone stands for. It stands beside the statement, not as its ground.
single.follows: For a thrown stone, falling is not bad and rising is not good.

single.quote: What is not good for the hive is not good for the bee either.
single.label: Hive and bee
single.t: What is not good for the hive is not good for the bee in it either.
single.why: Only this passage of the section speaks of a community and its member. Article 3 says that what serves the whole is good for every part; this passage says that what is not good for the whole is not good for the part. It does not contradict Article 3, and it is not the same claim. It stands beside the statement, not as its ground.
single.follows: A bee cannot gain from what does not benefit its hive.

single.label: Upright on my own
single.t: I am to be upright on my own, not held upright by someone else.
single.why: Only this passage of the section says it. The same rule ends modern 3.5 (Casaubon’s 3.6), which Article 22 quotes in its claim 2.
single.follows: Uprightness should be one’s own, not something that another keeps in place.

single.quote: The best way to fight back is to not become like them.
single.label: Fighting back
single.t: When I fight back against someone, the best way is not to become like them.
single.why: Only this passage of the section speaks of an opponent. The Greek does not say like whom; “them” stands for whoever is being fought.
single.follows: The best way to fight back against someone is to not become like them.

unfused.reason: The five passages of this section are separate short sayings, and no two of them say the same thing, so nothing here is fused. Four are kept side by side, each on its own; the fifth is half a sentence and is set aside.
