decisions: The editor recommended that this section get no article, since no two of its passages share a claim. It stands instead as four said-once items, so that the article numbers stay as planned; whether the section keeps an article is the owner’s decision.

The statement joins the two sayings about my own conduct (7.9 and 6.5) with a plain “and”. The stone (9.15) and the hive (6.49) are placed under Why as images that stand beside the statement, not as its ground, and each item says so.

Reads “not held upright” in 7.9 as not held upright by someone else, and writes “on my own”. The “not” itself is uncertain: according to the translators’ note it is a correction by an editor of the Greek text, and the manuscripts read “or”, a report the note marks as from memory and unchecked.

Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. 9.15 is 9.17 in modern editions, 7.9 is 7.12, 6.49 is 6.54, 6.5 is 6.6, and 8.40 is the end of 8.41.
articles.limit: This section has no common topic, and the article states two separate rules without arguing for either. Both are said elsewhere: Article 22’s claim 2 says my mind must stand upright by itself, not set upright by anything else, and Article 19’s said-once 7.36a, never to feel towards inhuman people what they feel towards human beings, is near not becoming like those I fight. The stone of 9.15 is near Article 34’s claim 4, that having fallen no more harms a ball, and the hive of 6.49 neighbours Article 3’s claim 2 and Article 8’s claim 5, that if the city is not harmed, I am not harmed. Seneca’s advice in Ep. 7.8 not to hate the crowd is already in Article 1; here only the clause on not copying the bad is used.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, being surprised at what happens gains a second author, and the article gains what Marcus leaves out here: what to do, which is to think ahead; what surprise costs; a way back after a loss; and words to say when wealth dazzles me. He limits the distaste for life as a whole, which must not turn into hating life, and he challenges the little breath: for him the soul is divine, not of one kind with dust and bones.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a task: I see to it that nothing is unexpected for me.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Let us be surprised at none of the things we were born to; no one should complain of them, for the very reason that they are equal for all.
piece.follows: We should not be surprised at any of the things we were born to, since they are equal for all.
piece.context: Letter 107: Lucilius’s slaves have run away, and Seneca answers that every trouble has happened to many. The “things we were born to” are the human lot of loss and death.
gives: or am surprised at any of them

items.label: action
items.t: I see to it that nothing is unexpected for me: thinking again and again about what may come keeps me from meeting any trouble as a new recruit.
items.why: In this section Marcus says that whoever is surprised at what happens is a stranger to the universe, but not what to do about it. Seneca says what to do: think about what may come, constantly. Article 3 has a similar item from Ep. 91.4.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: We must see to it that nothing is unexpected for us
support.follows: We should make sure that nothing is unexpected for us.
support.context: Letter 107, on bearing what life brings: the prepared meet hard things bravely, the unprepared take fright at the lightest. “Us” is anyone facing the troubles of life.
gives: I see to it that nothing is unexpected for me

support.author: seneca
support.quote: constant thought will secure this: that you meet no trouble as a new recruit.
support.follows: Constant thought lets us meet any trouble without being a new recruit to it.
support.context: Letter 107, on bearing what life brings: troubles are heavier for being new. The “trouble” is whatever may come; the “new recruit” is the one it catches unprepared, who takes fright.

items.label: breaks
items.t: What surprises me weighs on me more: newness adds weight to a misfortune, and I feel more pain from what also takes me by surprise.
items.why: Marcus says that being surprised shows I am a stranger to the universe; he does not say what surprise costs. Seneca says it adds to the pain.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: newness adds weight to disasters, and no mortal has failed to feel more pain at what also took him by surprise.
support.follows: A misfortune hurts more when it is new and comes as a surprise.
support.context: Letter 91: the city of Lyon has burned down, and the news has shaken Seneca’s friend Liberalis. The “disasters” are events like this fire.

items.label: breaks
items.t: When I lose something, I hold in memory what I had and the fruit I gathered from it. Having it can be snatched from me; having had it, never.
items.why: 11.29 shows what failing looks like, asking for a child who is no longer given, and gives no way back. Seneca gives one for every loss: to hold in memory what I had. It also tempers the distaste of claim 3: what I have enjoyed I hold in memory with thanks. Article 32 uses the same letter to limit its claim 3, that nothing passing is great.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: This: that we hold in memory the things lost, and do not let the fruit we gathered from them drop away along with the things themselves.
support.follows: Against our losses, our help is to remember what we lost and to keep the fruit we gathered from it.
support.context: Letter 98, on Fortune’s fickleness: Seneca has just quoted a consolation to a woman who lost her son. The “things lost” are whatever Fortune takes.
gives: I hold in memory what I had and the fruit I gathered from it

support.author: seneca

support.follows: What we have can be snatched away; that we have had it cannot.
support.context: Letter 98, on Fortune’s fickleness, in Seneca’s answer to every loss. “Having” is possessing a thing now; “having had” is the fact of having once possessed it.

items.label: practice
items.t: When a display of wealth dazzles me, I ask why I should marvel or be struck dumb at it: it is a procession, shown and not owned, and it passes by even while it pleases. Under the gold there is ugly timber.
items.why: Marcus sees costly things for what they are made of (9.34). Seneca adds words to say to myself when such a display dazzles me, and says that its splendour is only a surface.

Why are you struck dumb? It is a procession. Those things are shown, not owned, and while they please they pass by.”
support.follows: A display of wealth is nothing to marvel at: it is shown, not owned, and it passes even while it pleases.

items.t: Seneca knows the feeling of 6.41 from the inside. He says that we slide into having had our fill of doing and seeing the same things, with philosophy itself pushing us there, and he voices the complaint in the first person: “How long the same things?” He also warns that we must neither love life too much nor hate it too much. He says that what usually brings a life to hatred of itself is sluggish leisure, and that to one who ranges through the nature of things the truth never becomes distasteful. He is not consistent: in Ep. 77.6 a Stoic he praises tells a sick friend weighing death that even mere surfeit may make one wish to die.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Some people are overcome by having had their fill of doing and seeing the same things, and not by hatred of life but by distaste for it.
support.follows: Some come to want death not from hating life but from distaste for it, having had their fill of doing and seeing the same things.
support.context: Letter 24, on despising death: Seneca warns against a reckless craving for death. “Some people” are those who feel it from distaste for life; he counts himself among them.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: not to love life too much and not to hate it too much
support.follows: We need to be warned not to love life too much, and not to hate it too much.
support.context: Letter 24, on despising death: having armed Lucilius against the fear of death, Seneca warns him against loving or hating life to excess.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: To one who ranges through the nature of things the truth will never become distasteful: he will have his fill of false things.
support.follows: To one who ranges through the nature of things the truth never becomes distasteful; he has his fill only of false things.
support.context: Letter 78, to Lucilius, who is ill: once we know good and evil, life will not weary us. Here “the truth” is what one learns by ranging through the nature of things.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: what usually makes it hate itself is sluggish leisure
support.follows: What usually brings a life to hate itself is sluggish leisure.
support.context: Letter 78, to Lucilius, who is ill: a life that surveys great and divine things never tires of itself. Here “it” is a life, and the life brought to hate itself is the idle one.

items.t: Seneca does not hold that the soul is of one kind with the body. For him it is divine, mixed for a time with what is human and held back by what is heavy and earthly; it manages the body as a necessary burden and does not love it. In 9.34 the little breath changes out of water, dust and bones and back into them. The disagreement is narrower than it looks: Marcus’s word is “little breath”, the stuff of life, while Seneca speaks of the soul that thinks and goes to the gods. Seneca is not consistent on this: in Ep. 65.16 the soul longs to return to the elements of which it was once a part.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: When that day comes which is to separate this mixture of the divine and the human, I will leave the body here where I found it
support.follows: At death the mixture of the divine and the human in me will be separated, and I will leave the body behind.
support.context: Letter 102, on our immortality: Seneca gives the soul’s own words. “I” is the soul; “the divine” is the soul too, and “the human” the body.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Even now I am not without them, but I am held back by what is heavy and earthly.
support.follows: Even now the soul is not without the gods; it is held back by what is heavy and earthly, the body.
support.context: Letter 102, on our immortality, in the soul’s own words. By “them” it means the gods it will be given back to at death; “what is heavy and earthly” is the body.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: it is not the lover but the manager of the body too, as of a necessary burden
support.follows: The soul at its height treats the body as a necessary burden to manage, not as something to love.
support.context: Letter 92, on the happy life: the soul that has risen to the gods looks down on the body. “It” is that soul, and “the body” is its own.

passages.title: On accepting fate willingly
passages.text: Let us be surprised at none of the things we were born to; no one should complain of them, for the very reason that they are equal for all. I mean it: they are equal, for even what someone has escaped he could have suffered. And an even-handed law is not the one that all have come under but the one that has been passed for all. Let the mind be commanded to keep an even temper, and let us pay the taxes of mortality without complaint.

passages.title: On accepting fate willingly
passages.text: There is no one who has not gone more bravely to meet what he had long braced himself for and stood up even to hard things if they had been thought over beforehand; the unprepared man, on the other hand, has taken fright at even the lightest things. We must see to it that nothing is unexpected for us; and because all things are heavier for being new, constant thought will secure this: that you meet no trouble as a new recruit.

passages.title: On the burning of Lyon and expecting disaster
passages.text: All these things bend the spirit of our friend Liberalis, a spirit firm and unbowed against his own troubles. And he has not been shaken without cause: what is unexpected weighs more heavily; newness adds weight to disasters, and no mortal has failed to feel more pain at what also took him by surprise.

passages.title: On not depending on fortune’s gifts
passages.text: What help, then, do we find against these losses? This: that we hold in memory the things lost, and do not let the fruit we gathered from them drop away along with the things themselves. Having is snatched away; having had, never. It is a thoroughly ungrateful man who, when he has lost a thing, owes nothing for having received it. Chance snatches the thing from us but leaves its use and fruit with us, and this we ourselves have lost by the unfairness of our longing.

passages.title: On empty fears and true riches
passages.text: So this is what I say to myself whenever something of that kind has dazzled my eyes, whenever I come upon a splendid house, a well-groomed troop of slaves, a litter set on handsome bearers: “Why do you marvel? Why are you struck dumb? It is a procession. Those things are shown, not owned, and while they please they pass by.”

passages.title: On fussy style and the lure of wealth
passages.text: We marvel at walls coated with thin marble, though we know what sort of thing is being hidden. We cheat our own eyes, and when we have flooded ceilings with gold, what else are we rejoicing in but a lie? For we know that under that gold ugly timber is lurking. Nor is it only over walls or panelled ceilings that a thin ornament is stretched: the good fortune of all those you see striding loftily along is overlaid with gold leaf. Look inside, and you will know how much evil lies under that thin skin of rank.

passages.title: On facing feared troubles and death
passages.text: Some people are overcome by having had their fill of doing and seeing the same things, and not by hatred of life but by distaste for it. We slide into this with philosophy itself pushing us, while we say: “How long the same things? Of course I will wake, I will sleep, I will be hungry, I will be cold, I will be hot. Nothing has an end, but all things are linked in a circle; they flee and they follow. Night presses on day, day on night; summer ends in autumn, winter bears down on autumn, and is checked by spring. All things pass in such a way that they come back. I do nothing new, I see nothing new: at some point there comes nausea at this too.” There are many who judge living to be not bitter but superfluous. Farewell.

passages.title: On facing feared troubles and death
passages.text: Whichever of these you handle, you will strengthen your mind to endure either death or life; for we need to be warned and strengthened in both directions: not to love life too much and not to hate it too much. Even when reason advises making an end of oneself, the leap is not to be taken rashly or at a run.

passages.title: On bearing illness and pain
passages.text: For a life that is surveying so many varied, great, divine things cannot be overtaken by the sense of having had its fill of itself: what usually makes it hate itself is sluggish leisure. To one who ranges through the nature of things the truth will never become distasteful: he will have his fill of false things.

passages.title: On fame after death and the soul’s immortality
passages.text: Next, it does not let a narrow span of life be given to it. “All the years are mine,” it says. “No age is closed to great intellects, and there is no time that is not open to thought. When that day comes which is to separate this mixture of the divine and the human, I will leave the body here where I found it, and myself I will give back to the gods. Even now I am not without them, but I am held back by what is heavy and earthly.”

passages.title: On reason and virtue sufficing for happiness
passages.text: When it has raised itself to this height, it is not the lover but the manager of the body too, as of a necessary burden, and it does not put itself under the thing it has been set over. No one is free who is a slave to the body; for, even if you pass over the other masters that too much anxiety on the body’s behalf finds, the body’s own rule is hard to please and fussy.

claims.t: Everything in life is the same: it is now as it was in the time of those already buried. Watching it for a hundred years comes to the same as watching it for three.
claims.shared: 6.41 says that all things “are the same and from the same”; 9.12 that “everything now is as it was in the time of those we have buried”. Both say that things do not change from one time to another.
claims.changed: 9.12 says “those we have buried”; the claim says “those already buried”. 6.41’s “and from the same” is left out. The “these things” of 9.36 are, in the part of its chapter left out here, the cause and the matter of things; the claim takes them as everything in life.

support.follows: All things, wherever one looks, are the same and come from the same.

support.follows: Nothing is different now from how it was when the people we have buried were alive.

claims.t: Everything is foul in what it is made of. Underneath, each thing is water, dust, little bones and a goatish smell; even marble is a callus of the earth, and gold and silver are sediment.
claims.shared: 9.12 calls all these things “filthy in their matter”; 9.34 speaks of “the rottenness of the matter that underlies each thing” and says that “all the rest is of this kind”. Both say that what everything is made of is foul.
claims.changed: 9.12 does not say what “all these things” are; the claim reads them as everything, as 9.34 does with “each thing” and “all the rest”. 9.12 also calls these things familiar and lasting a day; the claim keeps only their matter. 9.34’s first list (water, dust, little bones, a goatish reek) fits a body, and its second (marble, gold, silver) fits things; the translators note that “each thing” could also be read “each person”. Of the second list the claim drops clothing as little hairs and purple dye as blood.

support.quote: All these things are familiar in experience, lasting a day in time, and filthy in their matter.
support.follows: These things are well known, short-lived and dirty in what they are made of.
gives: Everything is foul in what it is made of

support.quote: The rottenness of the matter that underlies each thing: water, dust, little bones, a goatish reek.
support.follows: The matter under each thing is rotten: water, dust, little bones and a goatish smell.

support.quote: Or again: marble is the earth’s callus, gold and silver are sediment, clothing is little hairs, and purple dye is blood, and all the rest is of this kind.
support.follows: Even costly things are made of lowly stuff: marble is hardened earth, gold and silver are sediment, and the rest is the same.

claims.role: Carrying one distaste to all of life
claims.t: The distaste I feel at the games, where the same things are always on show, or at the baths, with their oil, sweat and slimy water, I should feel about the whole of life: every part of it, and every object, is like that.

support.quote: Just as what goes on in the amphitheatre and places of that kind repels you, since the same things are always being seen, and the sameness makes the spectacle cloying, feel this way about the whole of life too.
support.follows: The weariness I feel at a show where the same things keep coming round, I should feel towards the whole of life.

How base and putrid, every common matter is! Water, dust, and

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 9.12 is 9.14, 9.34 is 9.36, 6.41 is 6.46, 8.23 is 8.24, 4.23 is 4.28–29 (the sentence quoted opens 4.29), 9.22 is 9.24, 12.10 is 12.13, 9.36 is 9.37 and 11.29 is 11.33.

Reads 9.36 as being about sameness. Its “these things” point back to the cause and the matter of things, in the part of its chapter left out here, which also asks what in them is new; the claim takes a hundred years and three as equal for that reason.
Reads the “little breaths carrying corpses” of 9.22 as the life in a person, as 9.34 uses “little breath”. 9.22 is a list with no verb and does not say what it is describing.

Follows the project English of 6.41, “feel this way about the whole of life too”, for claim 3’s “I should feel”. The Greek has a bare infinitive with no verb to govern it, and it can also be read as a statement: this is what happens to you with the whole of life too.
articles.limit: Article 3 already says that nothing that happens is unusual, and Article 34, claim 8, that the same things happen in every age, only with other people; what this article adds is the ground, that things are always the same and foul in their matter, and that being surprised at what happens shows I am a stranger to the universe. It pulls against Article 5, claim 3, where what looks rotten looks different, even pleasing, to someone who knows nature well: both are Marcus’s, and in the editor’s reading that one looks at matter with nature’s eye so as to accept it, while this one strips things down to their matter so as to stop prizing them. The article states a way of seeing and does not argue for it, gives no action beyond a feeling and a warning, and sets aside three of the twelve passages.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the claims on what my soul sees, on going straight towards its goal and on being ready when life ends gain a second author. “Practice” gains a review of the day, “When it breaks” gains the soul that turns from king to tyrant, which also extends the statement, and “If I doubt it” gains a reason to fear neither end nor crossing. He limits the claim on what is mine: the body is to be cared for with diligence, though not lived for.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement goes on to say what a soul that loses control becomes: it turns from a king into a tyrant, and uncontrolled passions take hold of it.

items.t: My soul is a king while it looks to what is honourable and gives the body no shameful command. When it is uncontrolled and greedy, it becomes a tyrant, and uncontrolled passions take hold of it.

items.t: Seneca does not call the body a corpse. He grants that holding the body dear is planted in us and that the body is in our guardianship. It should be cared for with the greatest diligence, he says, but we should not live for it, and should be ready to give it up when reason, dignity or good faith demands. This limits the claim that the soul carries the body like a corpse; it does not contradict it. He is not consistent: elsewhere he calls the body a necessary burden, to be managed, not loved (Ep. 92.33).

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I admit that holding our own body dear is planted in us; I admit that we act as its guardians.
support.follows: It is planted in us to hold our bodies dear, and we act as their guardians.
support.context: Letter 14, on withdrawing from the world. Seneca grants that we hold our bodies dear, then says we must not be their slaves; “its” in “its guardians” is our own body.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: This is how we ought to conduct ourselves: not as though we ought to live for the sake of the body, but as though we could not live without the body.
support.follows: We should treat the body as something we cannot live without, not as what we live for.
support.context: Letter 14, on withdrawing from the world. Seneca sets out how far the body is to be served: enough to keep it, never as the end of life.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Let it be cared for with the greatest diligence, but on the understanding that, when reason demands it, when dignity demands it, when good faith demands it, it must be thrown into the flames.
support.follows: We should take the greatest care of the body, and be ready to give it up when reason, dignity and good faith demand it.
support.context: Letter 14, on withdrawing from the world. The sentence closes his account of the body: care for it diligently, but be ready to throw it into the flames.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: it is not the lover but the manager of the body too, as of a necessary burden
support.follows: The soul treats the body as a necessary burden, to be managed and not loved.
support.context: Letter 92, on the happy life. “It” is the soul that has risen to the height Seneca has just described, set over all things; from there it looks down on the body.

passages.title: On fame after death and the soul’s immortality
passages.text: Say rather how natural it is to stretch one’s mind out into what has no measure. The human soul is a great and noble thing. It lets no boundaries be set for it except those it shares with god as well. First, it does not accept a lowly homeland, Ephesus or Alexandria or any ground there may be that is still more crowded with inhabitants or richer in buildings. Its homeland is whatever encloses the highest things and the whole of things in its circuit: this entire vault within which the seas and the lands lie, within which the air, while it separates the divine from the human, also joins them, in which so many divine powers are posted and stand watch, ready for their own work.

passages.title: On virtue as the only good
passages.text: Whenever you want to know what is to be avoided or what is to be aimed at, look to the highest good, the purpose set before your whole life. For whatever we do ought to agree with it: no one will put the particulars in order unless he already has the whole of his life set before him. No one, though he has his colours ready, will produce a likeness unless it is already settled what he wants to paint. The reason we go wrong is that we all deliberate about the parts of life, and no one deliberates about the whole.

passages.title: On virtue as the only good
passages.text: The man who wants to shoot an arrow must know what he is aiming at, and then direct and guide the shaft with his hand: our plans go astray because they have nothing to be directed at; no wind is favourable to one who does not know what harbour he is aiming for. Chance is bound to have great power in our life, because we live by chance.

passages.title: On facing feared troubles and death
passages.text: I am not so silly as to go through the Epicurean refrain at this point and say that the fears of the underworld are empty, that Ixion is not turned on a wheel, that no rock is pushed uphill by the shoulders of Sisyphus, that no one’s entrails can both grow back and be torn at every day. No one is so much a child as to fear Cerberus and the darkness and the ghostly look of those whose bare bones hang together. Death either consumes us or strips us bare. For those who are let out, better things remain, with the burden taken off; for those who are consumed, nothing remains: good things and bad alike have been removed.

passages.title: On being ready and willing to die
passages.text: I write you this letter in this frame of mind: as though death were going to call me away at the very moment of writing. I am ready to go, and I shall enjoy life for this reason, that I do not hang in too much suspense over how long this will last. Before old age I took care to live well; in old age I take care to die well. And to die well is to die willingly.

passages.title: On a daily routine and drunkenness
passages.text: So I will do what you tell me, and I will gladly write to you what I do and in what order. I will watch myself at once and, what is most useful, I will review my day. What makes us very bad is that no one looks back at his own life. We think about what we are going to do, and that rarely; we do not think about what we have done; and yet a plan for the future comes from the past.

passages.title: On style as a mirror of character
passages.text: Since I have used this comparison, I will keep to it. Our mind is at one time a king, at another a tyrant: a king when it looks to what is honourable, cares for the welfare of the body entrusted to it and gives it no command that is shameful, none that is sordid; but when it is uncontrolled, greedy, self-indulgent, it passes over to a hateful and dreadful name and becomes a tyrant. Then uncontrolled passions take hold of it and press on it; and at first, indeed, it rejoices, as a people commonly does when it is filled to no purpose with a handout that will harm it and paws at what it cannot swallow;

passages.title: On causes and the worth of studying nature
passages.text: The place that god holds in this world, the mind holds in a human being; what matter is there, the body is in us. So let the worse serve the better. Let us be brave against the things of chance; let us not tremble at wrongs, at wounds, at chains, at want. What is death? Either an end or a crossing. I am not afraid of ceasing, for it is the same as not having begun; nor of crossing over, because nowhere shall I be so cramped. Farewell.

passages.title: On caring for the body and staying safe
passages.text: I admit that holding our own body dear is planted in us; I admit that we act as its guardians. I do not deny that it should be indulged; I deny that we should be its slaves. For the man who is a slave to his body, who fears too much for it, who measures everything by it, will be a slave to many.

passages.title: On caring for the body and staying safe
passages.text: This is how we ought to conduct ourselves: not as though we ought to live for the sake of the body, but as though we could not live without the body. Too great a love of it unsettles us with fears, loads us with anxieties, exposes us to insults. What is honourable is cheap to the man to whom his body is too dear. Let it be cared for with the greatest diligence, but on the understanding that, when reason demands it, when dignity demands it, when good faith demands it, it must be thrown into the flames.

passages.title: On reason and virtue sufficing for happiness
passages.text: When it has raised itself to this height, it is not the lover but the manager of the body too, as of a necessary burden, and it does not put itself under the thing it has been set over. No one is free who is a slave to the body; for, even if you pass over the other masters that too much anxiety on the body’s behalf finds, the body’s own rule is hard to please and fussy.

claims.t: My soul sees itself, and it sees the whole: it goes round the whole universe and knows the reason that runs through all of it.
claims.shared: 11.1 and 11.11 both say that the soul sees itself (11.1: “it sees itself”; 11.11: it sees “the truth within itself”; the Greek verb is ὁρᾷ in both). 11.1, 11.11 and 5.26 all say that it takes in the whole: “the whole universe”, “the truth of all things”, “the reason that runs through the whole of substance”.
claims.changed: 11.11 says the soul sees this when it is true to its own form; the claim drops the condition. 5.26 speaks of the soul that has skill and understanding; the claim says “my soul”.

support.quote: it sees itself, it analyses itself
support.follows: The reasoning soul sees itself and analyses itself.

support.quote: shines with a light by which it sees the truth, the truth of all things and the truth within itself

claims.role: What is mine and what is not
claims.t: I am a soul and a body, and the soul carries the body like a corpse. Whatever is not my mind’s own activity is indifferent to it: dead things and smoke. All of its own activity is in its power, and everything lies in that.
claims.shared: 6.30 and 4.34 both say what I am made of, a body and a soul (“a little body and a soul”; “a little soul carrying a corpse”). 6.30 and 12.26 both set the mind’s own activity against everything else and dismiss the rest: it is “indifferent” in 6.30 and “dead things and smoke” in 12.26.
claims.changed: 6.30 calls the body little and 4.34 the soul; the claim drops “little” both times. 6.30 says “mind” and 12.26 “the ruling part”; the claim says “my mind” for both. 12.26 counts even what lies within choice among “the rest”; the claim keeps to 6.30’s line between the mind’s own activity and everything else. 4.34 makes me the soul and the body what it carries; the claim joins this to 6.30’s “made of a little body and a soul”.

support.follows: I am made of a small body and a soul.

claims.t: At every turn I ask myself how my ruling part is using itself now, and for what, and whether I have the soul of a child, a tyrant, a farm animal or a wild beast.
claims.shared: 5.11 and 12.26 ask the same question: how the soul, the ruling part, is being used (“am I using my own soul for now?”; “How is the ruling part using itself?”; the Greek verb is χρῆσθαι in both). 5.11 and 9.39 both name the beasts it can sink to: “a farm animal’s”, “a wild beast’s”; “turned into a wild beast”, “grazing”.
claims.changed: 5.11 says “my own soul” and names the ruling part a sentence later; the claim says “ruling part”, as 12.26 does. 9.39 is a question whose grammar can be read more than one way; the claim takes only its list of what the ruling part can become. 5.11’s youth and silly woman are dropped. 12.26 asks how the ruling part is using itself; 5.11 asks for what; the claim keeps both.

claims.t: My soul does violence to itself and becomes worse than itself when it is beaten by pleasure or pain, or when it pretends, saying or doing what it does not mean. Nothing I could find is worth that. I value nothing above my soul, and I do not make my good fortune depend on what goes on in other people’s souls.
claims.shared: 2.14 and 2.3 both say that the soul does violence to itself (the Greek verb is ὑβρίζειν in both). 11.1 and 2.3 both say that the soul should rank nothing above itself: 11.1 that it values nothing above itself, 2.3 by reproaching a soul that does not respect itself and puts its good fortune in other people’s souls.
claims.changed: 2.3 is a reproach; the claim states its opposite as what I do. 8.44’s four states (brought low, craving, shrinking in, taking fright) and 2.14’s other ways in which the soul harms itself are left out. The first sentence reads 2.14’s violence and 8.44’s worsening as one thing, so the conditions 2.14 names apply to both; 8.44 names its own states and does not speak of pretending.

support.quote: Do violence, do violence to yourself, soul

claims.t: When my life ends, my soul may be extinguished or scattered, or it may hold together. Whichever it is, my soul has reached its own goal at whatever point my life stops: the task set before it is complete, and it can be ready to leave the body this moment.
claims.shared: 11.1 and 11.3 both speak of the moment life ends and say the soul is complete or ready then (“wherever the limit of life comes upon it”; “if it must this moment be released from the body”). 11.3 and 4.17 both leave open what becomes of the soul, and both say it may “hold together” (συμμεῖναι in both).
claims.changed: “Whichever it is” is the editor’s, joining the two sentences. 11.1’s “end” (τέλος) is the soul’s goal, not its ceasing to be, so the claim says “goal”. 4.17 adds that souls which hold together do so only for a while and are then taken back into the whole; the claim keeps only that they may hold together. 11.3 says the soul is ready; the claim says it can be.

support.quote: it reaches its own end wherever the limit of life comes upon it
support.follows: Wherever the reasoning soul’s life is cut off, it has already reached its own goal.

claims.t: My mind does not move as bodies do, as an arrow flies or as the elements go up, down and round. Even when I am cautious or turning a question over, my mind still goes straight towards the target set before it. I let no action fly at random: even the smallest is done with reference to my goal.
claims.shared: 8.57 and 6.16 both set the mind’s or virtue’s movement apart from the movement of bodies: the arrow, and the elements going up, down and round (φέρεσθαι and φοραί, one root in the Greek). 2.14 and 8.57 both give the mind’s action a target: it is done “with reference to the end” and travels “towards what is set before it”.
claims.changed: “Bodies” is the editor’s word for the arrow and the elements together. 8.57 says the mind differs from the arrow in its manner (cautious, turning about) and still travels straight; the claim says the same. 6.16 speaks of the movement of virtue and 8.57 of the mind; the claim reads both as my mind’s movement. 2.14 counts aimless action among the ways the soul does violence to itself; the claim keeps only the aim. It says “goal” for 2.14’s “end”, which its next sentence defines as following the reason and law of the oldest city.

support.quote: Fifth, when it lets some action or impulse of its own fly at no target, but does anything whatever at random and without attention, though even the smallest things ought to be done with reference to the end.
support.follows: The soul harms itself when it acts at random; even the smallest things should be done with reference to the end.
gives: towards the target set before it
I let no action fly at random
even the smallest is done with reference to my goal

support.quote: Yet the mind, both when it is being cautious and when it turns about in considering something, travels straight none the less, and towards what is set before it.
support.follows: Even when it is cautious or turning a question about, the mind still travels straight towards what is set before it.

towards the target set before it

gives: My mind does not move as bodies do
as an arrow flies

support.quote: Up, down, round in a circle: such are the motions of the elements. The movement of virtue, though, is in none of these
support.follows: Virtue does not move as the elements move, up, down or round in a circle.
gives: My mind does not move as bodies do

single.quote: Things stand outside the doors, themselves by themselves, knowing nothing about themselves and pronouncing nothing. What, then, pronounces on them? The ruling part.
single.label: Things say nothing
single.t: Things stand outside the doors, on their own; they know nothing about themselves and pronounce nothing. It is my ruling part that pronounces on them.
single.why: Only 9.13 says that the ruling part pronounces on things. It comes close to the claim that sets the mind’s own activity apart from everything else, but no other passage here says who judges things.
single.follows: Things say nothing about themselves; whatever is said about them is said by the ruling part.

single.quote: The rational soul’s own are also love of those near it, and truthfulness, and a sense of shame
single.label: Its own virtues
single.t: Love of those near me, truthfulness and a sense of shame belong to my soul.
single.why: Only 11.1 names these as the soul’s own. 2.3’s “respect yourself” (αἰδεῖσθαι) is the verb from the same root as 11.1’s αἰδώς, “a sense of shame”, but 2.3 speaks of respect for oneself, not of a virtue the soul owns. The words that follow them in 11.1, valuing nothing above itself, are joined with 2.3 in the claim on how my soul harms itself.
single.follows: Love of those near it, truthfulness and a sense of shame belong to the reasoning soul.

single.quote: Someone who follows reason in everything is something at once unhurried and quick to move, at once cheerful and composed.
single.label: Following reason
single.t: When I follow reason in everything, I am at once unhurried and quick to move, cheerful and composed.
single.why: Only 10.14 describes the person whom reason leads. It says what such a person is like, not where the mind is going, so it is kept apart from the claim on going straight towards the goal.
single.follows: Whoever follows reason in everything is unhurried yet quick to move, cheerful yet composed.

single.quote: this readiness should come from a judgment of one’s own, not by way of bare opposition, as with the Christians, but in a reasoned and dignified way, and so as to convince someone else too, without theatrics
single.label: A reasoned readiness
single.t: My readiness to leave the body should come from my own judgment, not from mere defiance. It should be reasoned and dignified, of a kind that could convince someone else too, and without theatrics.
single.why: Only 11.3 says where the readiness should come from. The claim on the end of life says the soul can be ready; this says how the readiness is reached.
single.follows: Readiness to die should rest on one’s own reasoned judgment, not on bare defiance or on show.

single.quote: you will have no chance left to honour yourself. For each person has one life, and yours is almost finished
single.label: Time is short
single.t: I have one life, and it is almost finished. If I spend it doing violence to my soul, I shall have no chance left to honour myself.
single.why: Only 2.3 says that time is running out for the soul to honour itself. It is the urgency behind the way back from doing violence to the soul.
single.follows: Each person has one life; Marcus’s is almost over, and soon he will have no chance left to honour himself.

members.text:
The natural properties, and privileges of a reasonable soul are: That
she seeth herself; that she can order, and compose herself: that
she makes herself as she will herself: that she reaps her own fruits
whatsoever, whereas plants, trees, unreasonable creatures, what fruit
soever (be it either fruit properly, or analogically only) they bear,
they bear them unto others, and not to themselves. Again; whensoever,
and wheresoever, sooner or later, her life doth end, she hath her own
end nevertheless. For it is not with her, as with dancers and players,
who if they be interrupted in any part of their action, the whole action
must needs be imperfect: but she in what part of time or action soever
she be surprised, can make that which she hath in her hand whatsoever it
be, complete and full, so that she may depart with that comfort, 'I have
lived; neither want I anything of that which properly did belong unto
me.' Again, she compasseth the whole world, and penetrateth into the
vanity, and mere outside (wanting substance and solidity) of it, and
stretcheth herself unto the infiniteness of eternity; and the revolution
or restoration of all things after a certain period of time, to the same
state and place as before, she fetcheth about, and doth comprehend in
herself; and considers withal, and sees clearly this, that neither they
that shall follow us, shall see any new thing, that we have not seen,
nor they that went before, anything more than we: but that he that is
once come to forty (if he have any wit at all) can in a manner (for
that they are all of one kind) see all things, both past and future. As
proper is it, and natural to the soul of man to love her neighbour, to
be true and modest; and to regard nothing so much as herself: which is
also the property of the law: whereby by the way it appears, that sound
reason and justice comes all to one, and therefore that justice is the
chief thing, that reasonable creatures ought to propose unto themselves
as their end.
members.english: What is the rational soul’s own: it sees itself, it analyses itself, it makes itself whatever it wishes, it gathers for itself the fruit it bears (for the fruits of plants, and what corresponds to them in animals, are gathered by others), and it reaches its own end wherever the limit of life comes upon it. It is not as with dancing and acting and things of that kind, where the whole action falls short of its end if something cuts in, but at every part, and wherever it is overtaken, it makes what was set before it full and in need of nothing more, for itself, so that it can say: “I have what is mine in full.” Further, it goes round the whole universe and the void around it and its shape, and it stretches out into the boundlessness of time, and it takes in the periodic rebirth of the whole and considers it from every side, and it observes that those after us will see nothing newer and that those before us saw nothing more remarkable, but that in a way a person of forty, if they have any mind at all, has seen all that has been and all that will be, in that it is all of one kind. The rational soul’s own are also love of those near it, and truthfulness, and a sense of shame, and valuing nothing above itself, which is law’s own too. In this way, then, right reason and the reason of justice turn out not to differ at all.
members.greek: Τὰ ἴδια τῆς λογικῆς ψυχῆς· ἑαυτὴν ὁρᾷ, ἑαυτὴν διαρθροῖ, ἑαυτὴν ὁποίαν ἂν βούληται ποιεῖ, τὸν καρπὸν ὃν φέρει αὐτὴ καρποῦται (τοὺς γὰρ τῶν φυτῶν καρποὺς καὶ τὸ ἀνάλογον ἐπὶ τῶν ζῴων ἄλλοι καρποῦνται), τοῦ ἰδίου τέλους τυγχάνει, ὅπου ἂν τὸ τοῦ βίου πέρας ἐπιστῇ, οὐχ ὥσπερ ἐπὶ ὀρχήσεως καὶ ὑποκρίσεως καὶ τῶν τοιούτων ἀτελὴς γίνεται ἡ ὅλη πρᾶξις, ἐάν τι ἐγκόψῃ, ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ παντὸς μέρους καὶ ὅπου ἂν καταληφθῇ, πλῆρες καὶ ἀπροσδεὲς ἑαυτῇ τὸ προτεθὲν ποιεῖ, ὥστε εἰπεῖν· ἐγὼ ἀπέχω τὰ ἐμά. ἔτι δὲ περιέρχεται τὸν ὅλον κόσμον καὶ τὸ περὶ αὐτὸν κενὸν καὶ τὸ σχῆμα αὐτοῦ καὶ εἰς τὴν ἀπειρίαν τοῦ αἰῶνος ἐκτείνεται καὶ τὴν περιοδικὴν παλιγγενεσίαν τῶν ὅλων ἐμπεριλαμβάνει καὶ περινοεῖ καὶ θεωρεῖ ὅτι οὐδὲν νεώτερον ὄψονται οἱ μεθ’ ἡμᾶς οὐδὲ περιττότερον εἶδον οἱ πρὸ ἡμῶν, ἀλλὰ τρόπον τινὰ ὁ τεσσαρακοντούτης, ἐὰν νοῦν ὁποσονοῦν ἔχῃ, πάντα τὰ γεγονότα καὶ τὰ ἐσόμενα ἑώρακε κατὰ τὸ ὁμοειδές. ἴδιον δὲ λογικῆς ψυχῆς καὶ τὸ φιλεῖν τοὺς πλησίον καὶ ἀλήθεια καὶ αἰδὼς καὶ τὸ μηδὲν ἑαυτῆς προτιμᾶν, ὅπερ ἴδιον καὶ νόμου· οὕτως ἄρ’ οὐδὲν διήνεγκε λόγος ὀρθὸς καὶ λόγος δικαιοσύνης.

members.text:
A man's soul doth wrong and disrespect itself first and especially,
when as much as in itself lies it becomes an aposteme, and as it were an
excrescency of the world, for to be grieved and displeased with anything
that happens in the world, is direct apostacy from the nature of the
universe; part of which, all particular natures of the world, are.
Secondly, when she either is averse from any man, or led by contrary
desires or affections, tending to his hurt and prejudice; such as are
the souls of them that are angry. Thirdly, when she is overcome by any
pleasure or pain. Fourthly, when she doth dissemble, and covertly and
falsely either doth or saith anything. Fifthly, when she doth either
affect or endeavour anything to no certain end, but rashly and without
due ratiocination and consideration, how consequent or inconsequent it
is to the common end. For even the least things ought not to be done,
without relation unto the end; and the end of the reasonable creatures
is, to follow and obey him, who is the reason as it were, and the law of
this great city, and ancient commonwealth.
members.english: The human soul does violence to itself most of all when it becomes, so far as it lies with it, an abscess, a thing standing apart, and a kind of growth on the universe. For to be vexed at anything that happens is a standing apart from nature, in some part of which the nature of each of the other things is contained. Next, when it turns away from some person, or even moves against them with the aim of doing harm, as the souls of angry people do. Third, it does violence to itself when it is beaten by pleasure or by pain. Fourth, when it plays a part and does or says something in a feigned and untrue way. Fifth, when it lets some action or impulse of its own fly at no target, but does anything whatever at random and without attention, though even the smallest things ought to be done with reference to the end. And the end of rational living beings is to follow the reason and law of the oldest city and constitution.
members.greek: Ὑβρίζει ἑαυτὴν ἡ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ψυχὴ μάλιστα μέν, ὅταν ἀπόστημα καὶ οἷον φῦμα τοῦ κόσμου, ὅσον ἐφ̓ ἑαυτῇ, γένηται· τὸ γὰρ δυσχεραίνειν τινὶ τῶν γινομένων ἀπόστασίς ἐστι τῆς φύσεως, ἧς ἐν μέρει αἱ ἑκάστου τῶν λοιπῶν φύσεις περιέχονται. ἔπειτα δέ, ὅταν ἄνθρωπόν τινα ἀποστραφῇ ἢ καὶ ἐναντία φέρηται ὡς βλάψουσα, οἷαί εἰσιν αἱ τῶν ὀργιζομένων. τρίτον ὑβρίζει ἑαυτήν, ὅταν ἡσσᾶται ἡδονῆς ἢ πόνου. τέταρτον, ὅταν ὑποκρίνηται καὶ ἐπιπλάστως καὶ ἀναλήθως τι ποιῇ ἢ λέγῃ. πέμπτον, ὅταν πρᾶξίν τινα ἑαυτῆς καὶ ὁρμὴν ἐπ’ οὐδένα σκοπὸν ἀφιῇ, ἀλλ’ εἰκῇ καὶ ἀπαρακολουθήτως ὁτιοῦν ἐνεργῇ, δέον καὶ τὰ μικρότατα κατὰ τὴν ἐπὶ τὸ τέλος ἀναφορὰν γίνεσθαι· τέλος δὲ λογικῶν ζῴων τὸ ἕπεσθαι τῷ τῆς πόλεως καὶ πολιτείας τῆς πρεσβυτάτης λόγῳ καὶ θεσμῷ.

members.text:
What is the use that now at this present I make of my soul? Thus
from time to time and upon all occasions thou must put this question to
thyself; what is now that part of mine which they call the rational
mistress part, employed about? Whose soul do I now properly possess? a
child's? or a youth's? a woman's? or a tyrant's? some brute, or some
wild beast's soul?
members.english: “Just what, then, am I using my own soul for now?” Ask yourself this at every turn, and examine: “What do I have now in this part, the one they call the ruling part? And whose soul, then, do I have now? Not a small child’s, surely? Not a youth’s? Not a silly woman’s? Not a tyrant’s? Not a farm animal’s? Not a wild beast’s?”

That soul which is ever ready, even now presently (if need be) from
the body, whether by way of extinction, or dispersion, or continuation
in another place and estate to be separated, how blessed and happy is
it! But this readiness of it, it must proceed, not from an obstinate and
peremptory resolution of the mind, violently and passionately set upon
Opposition, as Christians are wont; but from a peculiar judgment; with
discretion and gravity, so that others may be persuaded also and drawn
to the like example, but without any noise and passionate exclamations.
members.english: What a soul it is that is ready, if it must this moment be released from the body, and either be extinguished or be scattered or hold together. But this readiness should come from a judgment of one’s own, not by way of bare opposition, as with the Christians, but in a reasoned and dignified way, and so as to convince someone else too, without theatrics.
members.greek: Οἵα ἐστὶν ἡ ψυχὴ ἡ ἕτοιμος, ἐὰν ἤδη ἀπολυθῆναι δέῃ τοῦ σώματος καὶ ἤτοι σβεσθῆναι ἢ σκεδασθῆναι ἢ συμμεῖναι. τὸ δὲ ἕτοιμον τοῦτο ἵνα ἀπὸ ἰδικῆς κρίσεως ἔρχηται, μὴ κατὰ ψιλὴν παράταξιν ὡς οἱ Χριστιανοί, ἀλλὰ λελογισμένως καὶ σεμνῶς καὶ ὥστε καὶ ἄλλον πεῖσαι, ἀτραγῴδως.

members.text:
Then is the soul as Empedocles doth liken it, like unto a sphere or
globe, when she is all of one form and figure: when she neither greedily
stretcheth out herself unto anything, nor basely contracts herself, or
lies flat and dejected; but shineth all with light, whereby she does see
and behold the true nature, both that of the universe, and her own in
particular.
members.english: The sphere of the soul is true to its own form when it neither stretches out towards anything nor runs together inward, neither coils up nor sinks in on itself, but shines with a light by which it sees the truth, the truth of all things and the truth within itself.
members.greek: Σφαῖρα ψυχῆς αὐτοειδής, ὅταν μήτε ἐκτείνηται ἐπί τι μήτε ἔσω συντρέχῃ μήτε σπειρᾶται μήτε συνιζάνῃ, ἀλλὰ φωτὶ λάμπηται ᾧ τὴν ἀλήθειαν ὁρᾷ τὴν πάντων καὶ τὴν ἐν αὑτῇ.

members.text:
If so be that the souls remain after death (say they that will not
believe it); how is the air from all eternity able to contain them? How
is the earth (say I) ever from that time able to Contain the bodies
of them that are buried? For as here the change and resolution of dead
bodies into another kind of subsistence (whatsoever it be;) makes place
for other dead bodies: so the souls after death transferred into the
air, after they have conversed there a while, are either by way of
transmutation, or transfusion, or conflagration, received again into
that original rational substance, from which all others do proceed:
and so give way to those souls, who before coupled and associated unto
bodies, now begin to subsist single. This, upon a supposition that the
souls after death do for a while subsist single, may be answered. And
here, (besides the number of bodies, so buried and contained by the
earth), we may further consider the number of several beasts, eaten
by us men, and by other creatures. For notwithstanding that such a
multitude of them is daily consumed, and as it were buried in the bodies
of the eaters, yet is the same place and body able to contain them, by
reason of their conversion, partly into blood, partly into air and fire.
What in these things is the speculation of truth? to divide things into
that which is passive and material; and that which is active and formal.
members.english: If souls go on existing, how has the air had space for them from eternity? And how does the earth have space for the bodies of those who have been buried over so long an age? For just as here the change and dissolution of these bodies, after they have gone on existing for a certain time, makes space for other dead, so the souls that pass over into the air, after holding together for a while, change and are poured out and are set alight, being taken back into the generative reason of the whole, and in this way they give space to those that come to settle there after them. That is what a person might answer on the supposition that souls go on existing. But one should consider not only the multitude of bodies buried in this way, but also that of the animals eaten every day by us and by the other animals. For how great a number is consumed and, in a way, buried like this in the bodies of those that feed on them! And yet the space takes them in, through their being turned into blood, through their alteration into what is airy or fiery. What is the way to inquire into the truth in this matter? Division into what is matter and what is cause.
members.greek: Εἰ διαμένουσιν αἱ ψυχαί, πῶς αὐτὰς ἐξ ἀιδίου χωρεῖ ὁ ἀήρ; πῶς δὲ ἡ γῆ χωρεῖ τὰ τῶν ἐκ τοσούτου αἰῶνος θαπτομένων σώματα; ὥσπερ γὰρ ἐνθάδε ἡ τούτων μετὰ ποσήν τινα ἐπιδιαμονὴν μεταβολὴ καὶ διάλυσις χώραν ἄλλοις νεκροῖς ποιεῖ, οὕτως αἱ εἰς τὸν ἀέρα μεθιστάμεναι ψυχαί, ἐπὶ ποσὸν συμμείνασαι, μεταβάλλουσι καὶ χέονται καὶ ἐξάπτονται εἰς τὸν τῶν ὅλων σπερματικὸν λόγον ἀναλαμβανόμεναι καὶ τοῦτον τὸν τρόπον χώραν ταῖς προσσυνοικιζομέναις παρέχουσι. τοῦτο δ’ ἄν τις ἀποκρίναιτο ἐφ’ ὑποθέσει τοῦ τὰς ψυχὰς διαμένειν. χρὴ δὲ μὴ μόνον ἐνθυμεῖσθαι τὸ πλῆθος τῶν θαπτομένων οὑτωσὶ σωμάτων, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ τῶν ἑκάστης ἡμέρας ἐσθιομένων ζῴων ὑφ̓ ἡμῶν τε καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ζῴων. ὅσος γὰρ ἀριθμὸς καταναλίσκεται καὶ οὑτωσί πως θάπτεται ἐν τοῖς τῶν τρεφομένων σώμασι, καὶ ὅμως δέχεται ἡ χώρα αὐτὰ διὰ τὰς ἐξαιματώσεις, διὰ τὰς εἰς τὸ ἀερῶδες ἢ πυρῶδες ἀλλοιώσεις. Τίς ἐπὶ τούτου ἡ ἱστορία τῆς ἀληθείας; διαίρεσις εἰς τὸ ὑλικὸν καὶ εἰς τὸ αἰτιῶδες.

members.text:
What art thou, that better and divine part excepted, but as
Epictetus said well, a wretched soul, appointed to carry a carcass up
and down?
members.english: You are a little soul carrying a corpse, as Epictetus used to say.
members.greek: Ψυχάριον εἶ βαστάζον νεκρόν, ὡς Ἐπίκτητος ἔλεγεν.

members.text:
Why should imprudent unlearned souls trouble that which is
both learned, and prudent? And which is that that is so? she that
understandeth the beginning and the end, and hath the true knowledge of
that rational essence, that passeth through all things subsisting, and
through all ages being ever the same, disposing and dispensing as it
were this universe by certain periods of time.
members.english: Why do unskilled and ignorant souls throw into confusion one that has skill and understanding? Which soul, then, has skill and understanding? The one that knows beginning and end, and the reason that runs through the whole of substance and, through all of time, manages the sum of things in appointed periods.
members.greek: Διὰ τί συγχέουσιν ἄτεχνοι καὶ ἀμαθεῖς ψυχαὶ ἔντεχνον καὶ ἐπιστήμονα; τίς οὖν ψυχὴ ἔντεχνος καὶ ἐπιστήμων; ἡ εἰδυῖα ἀρχὴν καὶ τέλος καὶ τὸν δι’ ὅλης τῆς οὐσίας διήκοντα λόγον καὶ διὰ παντὸς τοῦ αἰῶνος κατὰ περιόδους τεταγμένας οἰκονομοῦντα τὸ πᾶν.

members.text:
Sayest thou unto that rational part, Thou art dead; corruption
hath taken hold on thee? Doth it then also void excrements? Doth it like
either oxen, or sheep, graze or feed; that it also should be mortal, as
well as the body?
members.english: Do you say to the ruling part: “You are dead, you are ruined, you have turned into a wild beast, you are playing a part, you are running with the herd, you are grazing”?
members.greek: τῷ ἡγεμονικῷ λέγεις· τέθνηκας, ἔφθαρσαι, τεθηρίωσαι, ὑποκρίνῃ, συναγελάζῃ, βόσκῃ;

members.why: Its first sentence is about the many senses of ordinary words and a sight that is not of the eyes. Its second divides a person into body, soul and mind, each with its own share (sensations, impulses, principles), and it is the one passage here that keeps soul and mind apart; the article reads them as one and divides a person only into soul and body.
members.text:
To steal, to sow, to buy, to be at rest, to see what is to be done
(which is not seen by the eyes, but by another kind of sight:) what
these words mean, and how many ways to be understood, they do not
understand. The body, the soul, the understanding. As the senses
naturally belong to the body, and the desires and affections to the
soul, so do the dogmata to the understanding.
members.english:
They do not know how many things are meant by “stealing”, by “sowing”, by “buying”, by “being at rest”, by “seeing what must be done”, which is not done with the eyes but with a different kind of sight.

Body, soul, mind. To the body belong sensations, to the soul impulses, to the mind principles.
members.greek:
Οὐκ ἴσασι, πόσα σημαίνει τὸ κλέπτειν, τὸ σπείρειν, τὸ ὠνεῖσθαι, τὸ ἡσυχάζειν, τὸ ὁρᾶν τὰ πρακτέα, ὃ οὐκ ὀφθαλμοῖς γίνεται ἀλλ’ ἑτέρᾳ τινὶ ὄψει.

Σῶμα, ψυχή, νοῦς· σώματος αἰσθήσεις, ψυχῆς ὁρμαί, νοῦ δόγματα.

members.text:
I consist of body and soul. Unto my body all things are
indifferent, for of itself it cannot affect one thing more than another
with apprehension of any difference; as for my mind, all things which
are not within the verge of her own operation, are indifferent unto her,
and for her own operations, those altogether depend of her; neither
does she busy herself about any, but those that are present; for as
for future and past operations, those also are now at this present
indifferent unto her.
members.english: I am made of a little body and a soul. Now to the little body all things are indifferent, for it cannot tell a difference. To the mind, whatever is not its own activity is indifferent; and whatever is its own activity, all of that is in its power. Even of these, though, it is concerned only with the present, for its future and past activities are themselves already indifferent as well.
members.greek: Ἐκ σωματίου εἰμὶ καὶ ψυχῆς. τῷ μὲν οὖν σωματίῳ πάντα ἀδιάφορα· οὐδὲ γὰρ δύναται διαφέρεσθαι. τῇ δὲ διανοίᾳ ἀδιάφορα ὅσα μή ἐστιν αὐτῆς ἐνεργήματα· ὅσα δέ γε αὐτῆς ἐστιν ἐνεργήματα, ταῦτα πάντα ἐπ’ αὐτῇ ἐστιν. καὶ τούτων μέντοι περὶ μόνον τὸ παρὸν πραγματεύεται· τὰ γὰρ μέλλοντα καὶ παρῳχηκότα ἐνεργήματα αὐτῆς καὶ αὐτὰ ἤδη ἀδιάφορα.

members.text:
Do, soul, do; abuse and contemn thyself; yet a while and the time
for thee to respect thyself, will be at an end. Every man's happiness
depends from himself, but behold thy life is almost at an end, whiles
affording thyself no respect, thou dost make thy happiness to consist in
the souls, and conceits of other men.
members.english: Do violence, do violence to yourself, soul; but you will have no chance left to honour yourself. For each person has one life, and yours is almost finished, while you do not respect yourself but place your good fortune in the souls of others.
members.greek: Ὕβριζε, ὕβριζε σεαυτήν, ὦ ψυχή· τοῦ δὲ τιμῆσαι σεαυτὴν οὐκέτι καιρὸν ἕξεις· εἷς γὰρ ὁ βίος ἑκάστῳ, οὗτος δέ σοι σχεδὸν διήνυσται, μὴ αἰδουμένῃ σεαυτήν, ἀλλ’ ἐν ταῖς ἄλλων ψυχαῖς τιθεμένῃ τὴν σὴν εὐμοιρίαν.

members.text:
Is this then a thing of that worth, that for it my soul should
suffer, and become worse than it was? as either basely dejected, or
disordinately affected, or confounded within itself, or terrified? What
can there be, that thou shouldest so much esteem?
members.english: Is this worth it, that because of it my soul should be in a bad way and be worse than itself: brought low, craving, shrinking in, taking fright? And what will you find that is worth that?
members.greek: Ἆρα τοῦτο ἄξιον, ἵνα δι’ αὐτὸ κακῶς μοι ἔχῃ ἡ ψυχὴ καὶ χείρων ἑαυτῆς ᾖ, ταπεινουμένη, ὀρεγομένη, συνδυομένη, πτυρομένη; καὶ τί εὑρήσεις τούτου ἄξιον;

members.text:
What is the present estate of my understanding? For herein lieth
all indeed. As for all other things, they are without the compass of
mine own will: and if without the compass of my will, then are they as
dead things unto me, and as it were mere smoke.
members.english: How is the ruling part using itself? For everything lies in that. As for the rest, it is either within choice or outside it: dead things and smoke.
members.greek: Πῶς ἑαυτῷ χρῆται τὸ ἡγεμονικόν; ἐν γὰρ τούτῳ τὸ πᾶν ἐστι. τὰ δὲ λοιπὰ ἢ προαιρετικά ἐστιν ἢ ἀπροαίρετα, νεκρὰ καὶ καπνός.

members.text:
Under, above, and about, are the motions of the elements; but
the motion of virtue, is none of those motions, but is somewhat more
excellent and divine. Whose way (to speed and prosper in it) must be
through a way, that is not easily comprehended.
members.english: Up, down, round in a circle: such are the motions of the elements. The movement of virtue, though, is in none of these, but is something more divine, and, going forward by a road hard to make out, it fares well on its way.
members.greek: Ἄνω, κάτω, κύκλῳ φοραὶ τῶν στοιχείων, ἡ δὲ τῆς ἀρετῆς κίνησις ἐν οὐδεμιᾷ τούτων, ἀλλὰ θειότερόν τι καὶ ὁδῷ δυσεπινοήτῳ προιοῦσα εὐοδεῖ.

members.text:
The motion of the mind is not as the motion of a dart. For
the mind when it is wary and cautelous, and by way of diligent
circumspection turneth herself many ways, may then as well be said to
go straight on to the object, as when it useth no such circumspection.
members.english: An arrow travels in one way, the mind in another. Yet the mind, both when it is being cautious and when it turns about in considering something, travels straight none the less, and towards what is set before it.
members.greek: Ἄλλως βέλος, ἄλλως νοῦς φέρεται. ὁ μέντοι νοῦς καὶ ὅταν εὐλαβῆται καὶ ὅταν περὶ τὴν σκέψιν στρέφηται, φέρεται κατ’ εὐθὺ οὐδὲν ἧττον καὶ ἐπὶ τὸ προκείμενον.

members.text:
What is that that is slow, and yet quick? merry, and yet grave? He
that in all things doth follow reason for his guide.
members.english: Someone who follows reason in everything is something at once unhurried and quick to move, at once cheerful and composed.
members.greek: σχολαῖόν τι καὶ ἅμα εὐκίνητόν ἐστι καὶ φαιδρὸν ἅμα καὶ συνεστηκὸς ὁ τῷ λόγῳ κατὰ πᾶν ἑπόμενος.

members.text:
The things themselves that affect us, they stand without doors,
neither knowing anything themselves nor able to utter anything unto
others concerning themselves. What then is it, that passeth verdict on
them? The understanding.
members.english: Things stand outside the doors, themselves by themselves, knowing nothing about themselves and pronouncing nothing. What, then, pronounces on them? The ruling part.
members.greek: Τὰ πράγματα ἔξω θυρῶν ἕστηκεν αὐτὰ ἐφ’ ἑαυτῶν, μηδὲν μήτε εἰδότα περὶ αὑτῶν μήτε ἀποφαινόμενα. τί οὖν ἀποφαίνεται περὶ αὐτῶν; τὸ ἡγεμονικόν.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 2.14 is 2.16, 2.3 is 2.6, 11.11 is 11.12, 4.17 is 4.21, 4.34 is 4.41, 5.26 is 5.32, 9.39 is 9.39b, 6.30 is 6.32, 8.44 is 8.45b, 12.26 is 12.33, 6.16 is 6.17, 8.57 is 8.60, 10.14 is 10.12b, 9.13 is 9.15 and 3.16 is 3.15–16a; 11.1, 5.11 and 11.3 are the same.

Reads soul, mind and ruling part as one thing: 5.11 moves from the soul I use to “this part, the one they call the ruling part”, and asks about both together; 6.30 moves from “soul” to “mind”, and 12.26 says “the ruling part”. 12.26’s “that” (everything lies in that) is read as how the ruling part uses itself, not as the ruling part itself, as the translators’ note allows.
Uses 9.39 only for its list of what the ruling part can become, since its grammar can be read more than one way, and reads 6.16’s “movement of virtue” as the right movement of the mind.
Keeps six claims, more than usual, because the section has eighteen passages and each claim has words that at least two passages say.
articles.limit: Other articles say parts of this one: Article 4 that what rules in me moves itself, Article 2 that reason should lead, Article 1 and Article 21’s claim 5 that every act has an aim, Article 12 that I ask what I am using my mind for (claim 3 here), that I go straight towards a target (claim 6) and that my mind pronounces on things (9.13), Article 13 that nothing is better than the spirit within me (claim 4), and Articles 10 and 34 what death may turn out to be (claim 5). What this article adds is the use the soul makes of itself: everything lies in it, and it can do violence to itself. The article reads that violence as giving in to pleasure or pain, or as pretending, so Article 8’s “nothing from outside touches my mind” still stands. Claim 5 says without condition what Article 17’s claim 2 says only of a disciplined mind, and Article 35, like 2.3 here, warns that time can run out. 11.1 feeds three claims and a said-once item, so the article leans on one long passage, and the claim under “If I doubt it” answers a doubt about the soul’s survival, not about the statement itself.
